subtopic: CANCELLATION OF FEDERAL SHARE OF SEED GRAIN LOANS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: CANCELLATION OF FEDERAL SHARE OF SEED GRAIN LOANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a question to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National

Inquiries of the Ministry Resources. When will the government announce its decision on loans for seed grain to needy pioneer settlers in western Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Alvin Hamilton (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: CANCELLATION OF FEDERAL SHARE OF SEED GRAIN LOANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had hoped to make this announcement some time ago. I am glad to have the opportunity this morning to answer the question of the hon. member for Melville.
Between 1876 and 1925 the federal government advanced loans for seed grain, fodder for animals and other relief to needy settlers in western Canada. Supplementary advances which were made in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan between 1919 and 1923 were implemented on a 50-50 joint federal-provincial basis. These advances were secured by liens registered against the homesteads, pre-emptions and other lands of the settlers concerned.
From 1927 to the present time the total principal indebtedness has been reduced from $16 million to approximately $200,000, through an extended program of compromise settlements; outright cancellation where extenuating circumstances justified such action; tax and mortgage foreclosure proceedings, or reversion of the lands to the crown. All the liens registered against lands in British Columbia and Manitoba were discharged or released some time ago, and payments in respect of the remaining Alberta and Saskatchewan indebtedness have fallen off in recent years due to unfavourable crop conditions.
Investigation has revealed that the majority of the outstanding accounts are registered against marginal or submarginal farms owned by small unit operators, many of whom suffered severe crop damage during the past winter, and further payments would cause unwarranted financial hardship.
Therefore cabinet has granted approval for cancellation of the remainder of the federal share of seed grain indebtedness, and the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan have concurred in this recommendation with respect to the 1919-1923 joint federal-provincial advances.

subtopic: CANCELLATION OF FEDERAL SHARE OF SEED GRAIN LOANS
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, the practice is growing, apparently, for the ministry to make statements and announcements of policy on the orders of the day when, under our procedure, it is not possible to make the comments which the opposition should be entitled to make. I should think Your Honour would find it helpful to remind the ministers of this government that statements of this kind should be made on motions.

subtopic: CANCELLATION OF FEDERAL SHARE OF SEED GRAIN LOANS

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: CANCELLATION OF FEDERAL SHARE OF SEED GRAIN LOANS

Yesterday leave was given to the Secretary of State for External Affairs to make a statement in answering a question and there was an opportunity for comment. The answer which has given rise to the hon. member's point of order was, I think, rather long and perhaps more in the nature of a statement than an answer appropriate to the question that was asked.

subtopic: CANCELLATION OF FEDERAL SHARE OF SEED GRAIN LOANS
speechtext: On the point of order, I would point out that in the particular case today leave was not granted, and I would simply say to the Prime Minister that I should have thought that he, as the head of the government, would support the position we have taken.

speechtext:
I take it that observations are in order, and I also have a supplementary question. These old seed grain liens have been a burden for some producers in western Canada for a very long time. Over the years I have had some experience in negotiating settlements for producers having difficulty in making the required payments, and I must say in all fairness that the officials of the department have been most generous in scaling down the amount of the indebtedness so the farmers could meet their obligations. Now that the total amount is down to such a small figure as $200,000 I think the action of the federal government in cancelling the federal portion of the remaining debt is probably an efficient way to deal with the matter.
My supplementary question has to do with this point. I was wondering whether this welcome but rather limited statement as to the cancelling of the seed grain liens was the government's alternative to the western farm delegation which has requested deficiency payments.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Finance. In view of the statement made to the press last week by Major General Bruce Matthews, president of the Excelsior Life Insurance Company and president of the national Liberal federation, to the effect that he and members of his family have sold their interest in the Excelsior Life to American interests, would the minister tell the house whether the government has the power to prevent control of the assets of this company, totalling over $100 million and representing the savings of thousands of Canadian policyholders, from passing into foreign hands?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCELSIOR LIFE INSURANCE COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure it is a matter of regret on the part of all of us that the control of this fine old Canadian life insurance company should be passing out of Canadian hands. It is, however, a corporation which was incorporated under the laws of the province of Ontario in 1889. It did register with the federal authorities in 1897 and has operated under the normal federal supervision since that time, as do a few but very few provincially incorporated life insurance companies. But this gives parliament and the government no authority or jurisdiction in this situation. The legislation which I introduced in the autumn of 1957 and which was passed by parliament applies, of course, to life insurance companies under federal jurisdiction. Accordingly, neither parliament

Inquiries of the Ministry nor the government has any authority or jurisdiction to interfere with the transfer of control of this company to foreign hands.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there were discussions between General Matthews and the superintendent of insurance in relation to this subject. I did not discuss the matter personally with General Matthews, but I was made acquainted with the results of the discussions between the federal superintendent of insurance and General Matthews. The views of the federal authorities in this respect I think are well known, and the policy of the government is well known. There was some information asked of General Matthews by the superintendent of insurance, I am told, which General Matthews did not feel he was prepared to give. I point out, however, that this is a matter that falls under provincial rather than federal jurisdiction.

Mr. Chairman, in speaking on this item the other day I believe some of the remarks which were credited to me were erroneously recorded and the implications drawn from them were not correct; therefore I think I should not leave this particular impression.
We were very critical of the immigration policies as they affect the immigration of Chinese, and of the problems which have developed in the investigations now taking place into this sort of immigration. We were very surprised to note that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate appears to be either in charge of the department here or in very close connection with it. Rather than being chastised by the minister of immigration, I found that this task fell upon the former minister of immigration who proceeded to undertake this duty as either the minister or the ex-minister or the associate minister or whatever he considers himself to be.
Speaking of this, newspapers across the country picked up a chance remark which was made during the speech of another member and attributed it to me. I was reported to have said that the whole Department of Citizenship and Immigration is rotten. This was certainly not my intention. It was not in the context of my remarks. I have an

obligation to make it very clear that I do not consider this to be the case, and never did. I have the highest regard for the civil service in general, and though I am not familiar with most of the people in the civil service who are attached to the Department of Immigration I presume that their honesty and integrity are similar to those in the other branches of the civil service, and beyond reproach.
However, I still consider that the reported infractions of the Immigration Act as they affect Chinese citizens could not have been entirely unknown. We have been told according to newspaper reports that as many as 11,000 Chinese may have come to Canada illegally in the last number of years, and I suggest this is a matter that not only those officials in Hong Kong who are appointed on a part-time basis to carry out investigations and the questioning of applicants must have known about. There must have been officials elsewhere in the department who had some knowledge of irregularities through reports which must have come in continually over the years indicating that irregularities were taking place in the department. If we are to believe or even to suspect that such breaches of the immigration regulations have taken place, we can only come to the conclusion that there have been officials throughout the department who must have known or suspected that all was not as it should be.
I am not alone in drawing this conclusion. We have been told that over the years there have been continual releases of personnel in Hong Kong, particularly in the interpretation and investigation branch where local people were employed, and that from time to time problems were raised. One of the reasons we are so concerned about this matter is that we believe there should be no discrimination with regard to immigration into Canada. We think that the present law as it affects the Chinese people is discriminatory and not in keeping with what the Canadian people believe should be the case in a country free from discrimination, a country which treats people of all races and creeds as being equal.
If these stories are true, in connection particularly with the immigration of Asiatic people, then I think some overhaul of the department is necessary in order to see that these infractions do not take place in the future. This would mean to me that the act itself should be changed so it would not be necessary for these infractions to take place, or so that no encouragement should be given for them to take place.
We are concerned about this matter for another reason. We sat on a committee this year which investigated a situation that involved infractions of rules and regulations,
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration and I believe there have been infractions of these rules and regulations. While the R.C.M.P. have investigated those cases, with only one or two exceptions they have not been able to ascertain who was responsible for the infractions or even the extent of the infractions.
I believe this will be the situation in relation to the department of immigration. It does not seem fair to me that all the Chinese people in Canada should be suspect because there have been infractions of the immigration law. I do not think it is legitimate that a questionnaire should be circulated and that the Chinese people should be asked to make certain commitments and certain statements to the R.C.M.P. or anyone else that would not be asked of people of other nationalities or other new citizens. I think these practices are discriminatory, and I do not believe they should be engaged in. It would seem to me that one should at least be fair to the people who have come here. Most of those who came in, even if they came to this country legally, paid their money and expected that they would be allowed to stay here, and have since tried their best to be good citizens. I believe many of them have been here for some time now, and have proven themselves to be good citizens.
I am not saying anything in the House of Commons, and I do not intend to say anything here, that I would not say any place else. I have been accused recently, as have other members, of doing so. It seems to me a nice way of saying that you are abusing your parliamentary immunity. I do not know what this involves. I am not sure I even know what it is. I have never been shy about voicing my opinions in any place; I think this is a freedom to which Canadians are entitled, but I do not think that should be so here any more than anywhere else. If there is a regulation which gives us some preference I have not used it and do not intend to use it.
I think this matter is so serious that I believe the minister should set up a commission immediately to investigate it. I will talk to the Chinese people with whom I have come into contact about appearing before such a commission if I can assure myself that discrimination will not be used against them and that they can accept the guarantees which are given. To date I agree with the Chinese association in its statement that it will not ask the Chinese people to testify or appear because it does not believe they will be given that immunity which they were promised in such a half hearted way. If immunity is to be granted, let the minister say she will guarantee it and that the government will stand behind it.

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
In this country we do not have a fifth amendment. When people testify they do so knowing very well that anything said under oath may be used against them, and unless the minister can take responsibility for allowing this right which is given in one country in particular by the fifth amendment I do not believe these people will come forward to testify. I would be happy to ask those with whom I come into contact to do so, but I will only ask them to appear if they can be reasonably certain that the assurances given by the commission will be sufficient to prevent their deportation and arrest for infractions which have taken place.
We have no objection to those people who are involved paying the full penalty of the law, since presumably they broke it and received remuneration for doing so knowing well, I imagine, what they were doing. But if any immigrants came in on that basis they have a right to protection. If they come forward the minister should be able to solve a problem that has bothered the department for many years. I suggest that an investigation take place in the department. I am sure the minister has nothing to hide. The people should be given immunity so they could come forward and we could clear up the problem. We are a country relatively free of discrimination as to race, colour or creed, and this freedom should apply in the Department of Citizenship and Immigration.
If the minister sets up a commission I will examine the guarantees given, and if I am satisfied with them I will ask the Chinese people in my constituency and those I know elsewhere to come forward; but I will do so only if I am sure they will not be deported on the basis of their testimony.
Certain people throughout the department must have known about the situation. I condemn them for the stand they have taken. They could have made a report at any time, on which report I am sure the minister would have acted. If we can believe the newspaper reports, they failed to come forward. My condemnation does not apply to the average employee of the department for whom I have the regard I have for most members of the civil service.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REQUEST FOR REPORT ON MEETING OF FISCAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I wanted to embark on a different subject and that is why I thought I

should first give the hon. lady a chance to say anything she had to say at this point.
I wish to speak about the question of the amendment to the act to which the hon. lady referred in her opening statement the other day. As a preface to what I have to say I should like to read from Hansard of April 29, 1955, when I was the minister of this department and my estimates were before the committee of supply. Certain observations were made at that time by the hon. gentleman who is now Prime Minister of Canada about the act and the regulations under which the department was then and still is-and I emphasize "still is"-operating, because there has been no change of any substance made, as the hon. lady indicated herself quite clearly in her opening statement.
I do not want to read unnecessary extracts from the debate, so I will start at the end of the first column on page 3320. These are the words of the present Prime Minister then sitting in opposition as the hon. member for Prince Albert:
-I come to the other matters that were being discussed this afternoon, that is the regulations and the application of those regulations by the department. I think however much the minister may endeavour to explain them away, the regulations are unjustifiable in their present' form. They are interpreted according to the whim and caprice of the individual official. They bring about in consequence a denial of fundamental rights. They constitute in fact arbitrary lawlessness.
The Prime Minister went on to say as reported at page 3321:
If that is not done-
That is, some changes made.
-are we going back to the days of the star chamber where appointees of the crown sat, made their decisions and placed themselves above the law? That is my main criticism of the department of immigration today. I do not lay the slightest personal wrongdoing at the feet of the minister. But I do say that the minister, having inherited the department and having had seven or eight months to clear away these wrongs-and they are wrongs-we have a right to ask today, "What have you done? Why have you not acted? What is the reason that equity and law have been pushed aside and the arbitrary say-so of an individual in a department has been placed above the law of the land?"
For three years now the hon. gentleman who described the procedures and regulations of the department in those terms has had the final responsibility for the government of Canada, and no change whatsoever of any consequence has been made in what the Prime Minister when he sat over here described as "arbitrary lawlessness" and said the opposition had a right to ask:
What have you done? Why have you not acted? What is the reason that equity and law have been pushed aside and the arbitrary say-so of an individual in a department has been placed above the law of the land?

Those were serious charges by a very eminent member of the bar of Canada made five years ago, and for three of those five years that hon. gentleman has been Prime Minister of this country and has apparently continued to tolerate this arbitrary lawlessness, as he described it. I did not agree with the hon. gentleman at the time nor do I agree with him now, but that was presumably the view with which he was opposing the government. The hon. gentleman presumably said it with sincerity and meant it. I think we should ask the minister to tell us what arbitrary lawlessness that existed in the department when she became minister has been ended, and how it has been ended, and to described in detail what has been substituted for what the Prime Minister described in these words:
What is the reason that equity and law have been pushed aside and the arbitrary say-so of an individual in a department has been placed above the law of the land?
That is what the Prime Minister said was the state of affairs in the department. The hon. gentleman said that five years ago. It is true that the Prime Minister does not seem to remember this very well, because I have in my hand a document tabled in response to a motion I made for papers.
I read an article in the Toronto Telegram, a newspaper that is not notoriously unfavourable to the present administration. This newspaper published a series of articles by George Brimmell, one of their reporters, who came to see the minister and myself and a number of other people before he wrote the series. In one of the articles which appeared on March 11, 1960 Mr. Brimmell said:
In April, 1955, while he was in opposition, John Diefenbaker accused the immigration department of "arbitrary lawlessness" in its administration. He said the department was tangled in red tape which is "in some cases administered... by sawdust Caesars who believe they are above the law."
I might say that if this is examined in its context-and I have the context here-the hon. gentleman did not in those terms apply it to me although indirectly that application may have been intended. I would think it was rather intended to apply to the officials of the department. Mr. Brimmell's article goes on to state:
Mr. Diefenbaker said then that fundamental rights are denied because unjustifiable regulations were "interpreted according to the whim and caprice of the individual official."
If that was true in 1955, in what way had the situation changed since Mr. Diefenbaker assumed power in 1957?
This was published in a newspaper which I am sure is more friendly to the present government than any other newspaper in
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration this country today, and for good reasons having nothing to do with its being a newspaper.
If that was true in 1955, in what way had the situation changed since Mr. Diefenbaker assumed power in 1957?
This question was put to Mr. Diefenbaker's office by the Telegram.
They drew the Prime Minister's attention to this correspondence, and this was the reply:
A letter from the Prime Minister's executive assistant said that "Mr. Diefenbaker did not recall the specific occasion in question, nor did we have a copy of the clipping readily available for him"-
I make nothing of this. It is in Hansard; there was no question of a clipping. I continue:
"-and under all the circumstances, he felt it better not to comment."
Well, that may have been a very wise view to take. I must say that I put a motion on the order paper to get this correspondence and, because of the technical wording of my motion, I was told there was no such correspondence. I then got in touch with the Prime Minister's executive assistant who explained the circumstances to me-and very reasonably, I think-and gave me the full text of the letter that he in fact wrote to Mr. Brimmell. I would be quite prepared, if there is need to do so, to put the whole letter on the record, but the substance of it is given in the article and I do not think it would serve any particular purpose. I just wanted to be quite sure that I was not in any way being unfair in quoting only part of what appeared in this letter.
Now, my question is this. Does the minister, after two years in her present office, feel that the Prime Minister was right in 1955 when he described this department as being in a state of arbitrary lawlessness, and when he said that "equity and law have been pushed aside and the arbitrary say-so of an individual in a department has been placed above the law of the land"? Does the minister feel that this is the state of affairs that prevails in her department? If she does feel that, what has she done about it; because in so far as the enumeration which the hon. lady gave the other day is concerned, there was really nothing-perhaps to be completely fair I ought to recall what that enumeration was. These were the changes which the hon. lady said had been made since the present government took office. This is to be found at page 4711 of Hansard of June 9, 1960. They are numbered, and read as follows:
1.	One of our first moves after taking office was to change the regulation which had formerly prevented Canadian residents of Asian origin from sponsoring the admission of their spouses and children until they became Canadian citizens.
5004	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
This, it is true, did make it possible for certain persons who had not previously been allowed to apply for their relatives, to apply for them, but it did not change in any way the conditions attendant upon those applications, so that if those applications were decided by arbitrary lawlessness before, this made no difference; it merely provided a few more cases which could be decided by the arbitrary lawlessness. So this could not have removed the arbitrary lawlessness that the Prime Minister was so eloquent about in those days when he occupied a position of irresponsibility, sitting over here on this side of the house.
2.	Next, the immigration appeal board was strengthened and its scope expanded.
Well, I would be quite interested to hear in what way the immigration appeal board, which I set up, has been strengthened. Perhaps when the hon. lady replies she can indicate how it has been strengthened. Has it been strengthened in personnel; has it been given any greater powers than it had before, or has it been given any greater scope? I understand it has been given greater scope. At a later stage I want to ask a few specific questions about that additional scope.
I took the view, when I recommended that the immigration appeal board should be set up, that under the terms of the act there was really nothing that could be adjudicated by a board in the normal sense of the word "adjudication" except with respect to landed immigrants; that landed immigrants, once they were landed, had certain rights in this country and their rights ought to be protected, and should be given the power to appeal where they could be represented by counsel who would be there to protect those rights. I also took the view that persons who were not landed immigrants but who happened to be visitors and were ordered deported, could hardly form a useful subject of any adjudication because there were no rights involved. What was involved was a judgment which this parliament saw fit, when the Immigration Act was last enacted, to impose upon the minister and ultimately upon nobody else. And even though the minister, or I when I was minister, might wish to take away those appeals from the minister altogether we could not have done it because parliament imposed that duty upon us and we had to perform it. We could get someone to assist us and that is what the board, and that is all the board, can do under the law as it now stands.
I am sure the hon. lady will agree with that without any question. So any arbitrary lawlessness that may have existed, to use the words of the Prime Minister, certainly could


not have been taken away by any change in the immigration appeal board, because the immigration appeal board in the past had jurisdiction to hear all the cases of those persons who had rights under the act, and to hear them publicly and with counsel representing them.
The third change the hon. lady referred to was:
3.	A new policy governing temporary residents of Canada was announced in August, 1958 which made it possible to regularize the status of several thousands of persons who had previously entered the country on a non-immigrant basis.
Well, now, lest the hon. lady try to get away with any view that this would take away that arbitrary lawlessness, it was, of course, just another arbitrary regulation, and a regulation which I consistently refused even to consider when I was minister. I am wrong in using the term "regulation"; it was an edict of the hon. lady. It is not a regulation. There is nothing in the regulations to say that after a certain date which escapes me at the moment, I think early in 1959, visitors would not be processed in Canada but would have to go back home and reapply.
That was, in my view, an arbitrary act by the minister. I said so at the time; I condemned it the other day when I was speaking, and I still think it is a very unfortunate policy which ought to be changed. But in no way could it have been said to reduce any arbitrary conduct there may have been in the past. It certainly was an increase of it. I think it was an arbitrary act.
4.	In co-operation with the provinces, significant improvements were made in measures providing for the welfare of immigrants after arrival.
I congratulated the hon. lady when she announced those changes and I am very happy to congratulate her again. This was a policy in which I took a great deal of interest when I was in the department, and my predecessor also took an interest in it. I am very glad the hon. lady has gone on in that direction because I think, speaking generally, the provincial governments, because they are in this business and Canada is not, have much better agencies for looking after welfare, and that it is much better to make arrangements with the provincial governments to have this done wherever it can be done on a satisfactory basis. I think the steps taken by the hon. lady in this field were progressive ones, just as I think those that we took previously also were progressive.
5.	Another important change, which I announced to the house only last month, simplified the arrangements by which residents of Canada may bring fiancees to this country.

Of course that is just an administrative arrangement. There is really no provision for this in the regulations at all. I think what the hon. lady did was a very sensible thing, but it was just another step in the direction of liberalization which has gone on steadily over the period since the Chinese immigration act was repealed in 1946. It had nothing whatever to do with the so-called arbitrary lawlessness to which the Prime Minister referred when he was over here in the speech he made in April, 1955.
I think the time has come when the minister should tell us whether she thinks the Prime Minister was right. Mind you, the Prime Minister was not talking about the minister at that time. I read the paragraph where he said he specifically exempted the minister from any wrongdoing. He was talking about the regulations and about the officials who administer the regulations when he described this situation as a state of arbitrary lawlessness. If it was a state of arbitrary lawlessness in 1955, surely a prime minister who is going to keep us here to consider a bill of rights later this session ought to do something first about rights which five years ago he said were not being respected. I do think we are entitled to know from the minister whether, in the light of experience, she at least thinks the Prime Minister was wrong in what he said in 1955.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REQUEST FOR REPORT ON MEETING OF FISCAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when this
estimate was last before the committee I had spoken for only five minutes when the adjournment hour came. I dealt briefly with the question of the deputy minister taking office, and I said at that time that I was going to direct the attention of the house to a few matters that had been brought to my attention by my constituents in general, by veterans, Legion branches, trade unionists and members of the Chinese community in my constituency. I am going to do so now as briefly as possible.
Before proceeding further I wish to emphasize once again that we believe a great deal of the dissatisfaction with immigration into Canada at the present time arises because we do not have a planned immigration policy. I do not underestimate all the difficulties. I have had a lot to do with immigrants from various countries. I do not underestimate the difficulties at all, but we do suggest that the greater part of our trouble arises from the fact that we have no planned immigration policy.
We in this group believe that immigrants should be processed at their point of origin, and that when it is decided that they are qualified to come forward they should be
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration brought here only when employment and housing are available. As long as we continue this hit-or-miss policy we will find immigrants

and I do not blame the immigrants -taking jobs away from Canadians who are unemployed when the immigrants arrive, or competing with Canadians for housing that is in short supply. We think this is most unfair, particularly to unemployed Canadians, because we believe our first responsibility is to Canadians. While we have an over-all responsibility to accept as many people in Canada as we can properly absorb, our first responsibility is to Canadians and at the present time to the nearly half a million Canadians who are unemployed.
I suppose it is because of the unplanned immigration policy and its effects throughout the years, particularly in recent months in the light of unusually high unemployment, that I have received a number of letters very critical of our immigration policy. The present policy at times creates unnecessary ill will. As I have brought to the attention of the house before, a case came to my notice just a year ago involving a man born in the city of Nelson. He brought up his family there, served and fought for this country for five years, has four children and was unemployed for six months. Day after day he went to the unemployment insurance office seeking work. I do not blame the immigrant in this case, but this is the sort of situation that creates ill will on the part of Canadians and is unfair to the immigrants as well. A job is open and this unemployed Canadian finds it being taken by an immigrant from another country, who arrived two days before.
Therefore I want to emphasize the point of view of this group that we believe there has to be a planned immigration policy to provide for the bringing forward of these people at a time when they can be employed, or can go to relatives who will guarantee to maintain them until they can obtain employment through normal channels, and at such time as they can obtain housing without competing with Canadians for housing which is in short supply in certain areas.
In that connection I want to mention another matter that has been brought to my attention by various unions in my constituency and also by farmers' representatives and others. I refer to the view, in which we in this group believe, that all employment placement should be the responsibility of the national employment service. We do not agree with the division of responsibility for the placing in employment of unemployed persons. The national employment service is there and its officials are trying to do a good job. They are not provided with the facilities
5006	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration to travel throughout every district in order to find employment for people from day to day.
I am not blaming the immigration officials for the situation, but it is their responsibility and they work hard at carrying it out. They are instructed to travel throughout their districts in order to secure employment for immigrants who are going to arrive within a few days or a week. Very often the immigration official arrives at a mill, a lumber camp or a mine and finds that there is a job open. As a result an immigrant who has been in Canada only a few days gets the job in the lumber camp, mill or mine while in the same district there are unemployed Canadians, some of them veterans, who in some cases have had their names registered with the national employment service for months.
Therefore I suggest that all employment placement should come under the direction of the national employment service, in fairness to the Canadian unemployed and in fairness to immigrants who often incur unnecessary ill will, which is understandable when citizens who have been unemployed for a number of months find that under their noses someone steps in and takes a job. In fairness to all concerned we think our suggestion should be adopted.
In speaking this morning I am not just giving my own views but am expressing the views of various groups in my constituency, as I have said before. We think a planned immigration policy based on sound principles should give consideration to all citizens within the commonwealth. There is no doubt that at the present time there is gross discrimination against persons coming from certain sections of the commonwealth. While we deny entry to Canada at the present time to a coloured person from another section of the commonwealth who may have fought for freedom against nazism, we allow some nazis of low repute into this country.
I get that information not from trade unions but from persons of German origin who were in Hitler's concentration camps and in a few cases from employees of one or two of Krupp's subsidiaries that are operating in Canada today. We let these people in without any question at all, and to indicate the unfairness of this policy I am going to refer to a matter I brought to the attention of the house on June 26, 1954. Personally I feel very strongly about this question. At that time during the debate on the estimates of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration I brought to the minister's attention the fact that five persons had been admitted to Canada who had been sentenced by the French government either to death or to long imprisonment.


The first was found guilty of anti-national actions against France and sentenced in absentia to imprisonment at hard labour for life and to national degradation for life, July 3, 1945, by the court of justice of Agen. The second was sentenced to five years imprisonment and to national degradation for life by the court of justice of Toulouse for collaborationist sentiments. The third was sentenced in absentia to the death penalty and forfeiture of all his property for treason on January 10, 1945, by the court of justice of Toulouse. The fourth was sentenced in absentia by the court of justice of La Haute-Savoie to imprisonment at hard labour for life, national degradation for life and forfeiture of all property, on February 26, 1946, for collaboration with the enemy. The fifth was sentenced on March 28, 1945, in absentia to death as guilty for dealings in time of war with a foreign power with a view to encouraging that power against France. He was an inspector in the Waffen S.S., and that means he was serving the German gestapo very well indeed.
All these men entered Canada under false names, with false passports, and were provided with false visas. I might say that a high French government official stated that they belonged to an organization that murdered the French minister, Georges Mandel, in the forest of Fontainebleau, massacred resistors, and betrayed allied parachutists who were hidden by brave Frenchmen. These parachutists may have included some of our own men.
At that time, I went on to deal with the matter at greater length. I might say the French government of the day requested the government of Canada to deport these people to France. We were supplied with the judgments by representatives of the French government; that is why I have them, and with the evidence. The French government was deeply concerned about this. I can remember reading the evidence in one case, and one of these men who is today a Canadian citizen was found guilty of hanging his brother Frenchman from a hook in a small cell, in the presence of the gestapo, applying a blowtorch and burning his body in various places, in an effort to get him to reveal the identity of other members of the underground.
There was similar evidence with respect to the others. These people were admitted to this country and were granted citizenship at that time. As I said before, these people now have the right to say "I am a Canadian citizen". We in this group protest very strongly indeed against this action on the part

of the Canadian government, because it indicates a type of thinking and discrimination which we feel is totally unjustified and most unfair.
At that time we admitted persons of this type, and there are others like them. I have had correspondence with a very interesting employee of the Krupp interests who gave information about some of these people. I do not question any normal citizen who had to fight for his country. However, we have let a few nazi beauties into this country, yet at the same time we have denied entry to a poor girl like Miss Rebrin, whose case is now before the courts so I am not allowed to say much about it. I have received letters from Francis Noel-Baker and a number of other people pointing out what they consider to be the injustice in this case.
I mention these things to illustrate the unfairness at the present time. I might say these people were admitted at the discretion of the minister of the day, by order in council. These people were considered fit to become Canadian citizens. In fact the minister has the power under section 10 of the Canadian Citizenship Act, which reads:
The minister may. in his discretion, grant a certificate of citizenship to any person who is not a Canadian citizen and who makes application for that purpose and satisfies the court that,
(b) he has been lawfully admitted to Canada for permanent residence therein;
(d) he is of good character;
I should like to see how anyone could consider the people I have mentioned to be of good character. I have documentary evidence to support my argument, because at that time the French ambassador supplied us with the information and indicated to us the indignation of the French government of the day.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I mention these matters briefly to indicate the practice of discrimination. I do not say these cases happened under the jurisdiction of the present minister-it was the prior government-but the same principle applies. It is the principle of gross discrimination against citizens of the commonwealth and orientals in general, as well as other good citizens, who are prevented from entering or residing in this country on the basis of very flimsy evidence indeed.

I wonder whether the hon. gentleman, before he passes on to another topic, would permit me to ask him one question. As I listened to him I gathered that his argument was that there should be no discrimination as between the countries of the commonwealth, from which I think one would 79951-0-316

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration infer that immigrants from the commonwealth would have preference over immigrants from other places. However, the hon. member for Timiskaming said that the principle of his party was that there should be no discrimination regardless of the place from which people come. Which is the policy of his party?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REQUEST FOR REPORT ON MEETING OF FISCAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: I suspected what the hon. member's question was going to be when he rose. Our policy is the principle nondiscrimination, applied with intelligence and common sense. When you say "non-discrimination", that does not mean you could bring into this country, suddenly, large numbers of persons of other races and other colours and retain the proper economic and social atmosphere. The hon. member knows exactly what we mean. We mean that we are opposed to discrimination in principle. We believe in the government making every effort possible to overcome it. We believe in a common sense approach to the problem, therefore the hon. member knows we would not suggest for a moment that, let us say, five million Asiatics should be admitted to Canada next year, or anything of that sort.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REQUEST FOR REPORT ON MEETING OF FISCAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: You preach a perfect paradox.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REQUEST FOR REPORT ON MEETING OF FISCAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: You believe in non-discriminatory discrimination.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REQUEST FOR REPORT ON MEETING OF FISCAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The hon. member mentioned the perfect paradox, but I note that he is only the parrot.
I must go on to mention the brief presented by the Chinese benevolent association from its national headquarters, 108 Pender street, Vancouver, British Columbia. I am not going to read this brief. There has been a considerable amount of discussion of this question, and I am not going to be repetitious and restate this case. This brief makes certain representations to the minister with respect to the recent allegations by officials of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. I do urge the minister to give serious consideration to these representations. We have not a large representation of Chinese in the district from which I come. I have known the older ones for many years, and I believe there are only 200 or 300 in Kootenay West. They make very good citizens. I have noticed one very interesting aspect of their life, and that is that you never find them applying for government assistance. They always manage to look after themselves or one another.
I do want to read the concluding paragraph of this brief, which has this to say:
Now be it therefore resolved that the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration be called upon to clarify the position of her department on the recent allegations in the press so that the misleading
5008	HOUSE OF

impression that there is a community-wide conspiracy to land immigrants illegally and use them for slave labour may be corrected or clarified.

We do not believe in strings of any kind. We call this non-discrimination with common sense, as I said before.
Mr. Chairman, there is one other matter I wish to bring to the attention of the committee and that is the question of landed immigrants, which has been raised several times before by hon. members of all parties. I am referring to how people from the United States come to this country and register as landed immigrants but have no intention of staying here. This happens mostly with construction workers, people who work on pipe lines and things like that. As a matter of fact I saw in the newspapers recently that the foreman of the crew putting in the gas pipe line to serve the restaurant and cafeteria of this House of Commons is a United States citizen. I thought that was most interesting, but I presume there is not a single man unemployed and available in Canada who could do that job and that is the reason this man is here. I am sure the minister will be able to give us that assurance when she speaks in reply.
We can all understand the case of a genuine landed immigrant, but in my constituency these United States citizens come to Canada as landed immigrants and therefore have a right to get employment as such. They work here for three or four months and then they go back again. What can we do about that? I think that is a question which has to be given consideration in fairness to Canadian citizens. This landed immigrant business has been worked to the limit in some places, with hundreds and hundreds of them coming across the line.
Mr. Chairman, let me tell you how I proved this on one occasion. In British Columbia if you are going to become a landed immigrant you are required to take out a licence for your car; if you are only a visitor you get a visitor's permit and are not required to take out a licence for some months. I asked the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to check up on some of these landed immigrants; not one of them had taken out a Canadian licence but all had visitors' permits. I think that is a section of the act which does want redrafting and drawing much tighter than it is now, in fairness to all Canadians.
In conclusion let me say that the members of this group realize the necessity for a complete revision of the Immigration Act. We realize that this is no light task and that there are many angles to be considered. I do not suppose there are many acts which present as many problems in drafting as a revised Immigration Act, and I well recognize that. But I think it is essential-

Mr. Chairman, since last week when we were discussing these estimates I have had occasion to submit some questions to the minister, and I want to take advantage of this opportunity to congratulate her department and her officials for the speed and accuracy with which some rather complicated questions were so efficiently dealt. I must confess that I did not expect a reply to be given within 24 or 48 hours, but I was delighted to see that the department's records are so well and accurately kept and I was pleased they were made available to me so quickly.
At the same time I would like to say that I was pleased to see from these replies that no deportations were ordered to iron curtain countries or to African countries. It certainly does disclose the attitude of the immigration department in safeguarding human lives, and I think there is no other department which has such humanised laws. The hon. member who has just taken his seat also used that term.
I would like to touch on the same subject matter the hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate touched on when he spoke of the facilities which should be given to people who are deported and wish to take their cases before the courts. I would refer, as did the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, to statements made on previous occasions by the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Justice. They argued very logically, forcefully and humanly when they were sitting on this side of the house that people should be told what they are accused of or what they are convicted of, virtually, when they are ordered to be deported and they are not now given the reason.

I do not know whether there is a difference in that regard between landed and non-landed immigrants, but I want to refer to a statement made by the present Minister of Justice on August 7, 1956, when he was sitting in opposition. I have not the full quotation from Hansard because I will only read that part which I think is applicable. As reported on page 7162 of Hansard for August 7, 1956, he said:
I refer, of course, particularly to the refusal of the department to inform prospective immigrants who are rejected of the reasons for their rejection, which practice is carried over in a number of cases to a refusal to inform people who land in Canada and against whom orders for deportation are made of the reasons for those orders. We have said before and we say again that this practice is absolutely unjustified and that it is contrary to the principle of justice upon which this country's system rests.
The Minister of Justice straightforwardly and, I was about to say, very nobly, declared that to place an immigrant in a position where he is virtually convicted, the sentence being to leave the country, without being given the reason is to do something which militates against decency and good judgment. It is possible that this may have been necessary during time of war in order to preserve Canadian security. It may be that this practice was determined during the last war, or at the end of the war. I do not know; but surely at the present time it is no longer necessary.
That is another reason why the minister should give active consideration to revising the act, and I say revising rather than amending because the minister told us a few minutes ago why it would be difficult to amend the act. I point out to her that the act was last revised in 1953, at which time some basic changes were made. I think the time has now come when she should accelerate the attention she is giving to the complete revision of the measure.
I do not know whether parliament gets the full facts when decisions or rulings are made by regulation or order in council. Members of this house do not have placed before them the regulation which decides or the rule which modifies the conditions under which an immigrant can enter the country. When I asked in my question the other day for departmental decisions as to cases, I was not concerned with the departmental decision on any particular case. It seemed to me that a decision is made in one case and that in the course of time it determines other cases as well; it becomes a standard.
I was not pinpointing any particular case. I was asking if there were departmental decisions of this type. If I am not correct about that-and the minister has indicated that I
5010	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration might be in error-then I should like the position to be made clear. Those are the type of departmental decisions that I mean. I do not even know that any exist, but I want to make sure whether there are any which are being used as standards affecting immigration into this country.
Let us take, for example, the statement the minister made on August 23, 1958 with respect to people who were in Canada as non-immigrants, and who were here for six months or a year. The minister wisely and humanely decided to let those people apply. I do not know whether that decision was made by order in council or by the minister herself. The first time we heard about it was when the minister announced it.
Take the announcement made by the minister recently with respect to fiancees. Was that done by order in council or was it a decision of the minister or a decision of the department to give some relief in this direction? I am not criticizing that decision. On the contrary, I praise it; but I am wondering why decisions of that kind are not placed before parliament for approval or rejection or amendment.
That is why I have asked so many questions on these matters. We do know that cases where the circumstances appear to be identical are, on occasion, decided differently with the result that people are left wondering. There may, of course, be circumstances on the files which are not disclosed but which would explain the difference in the decisions, but I think these circumstances should be disclosed in order to avoid any misunderstanding or even harsh thoughts about what has happened. People are human. They may inadvertently have some unkind thoughts when they see two cases where the circumstances appear to be identical decided in different ways.
I present these thoughts to the minister not with a view to being critical but in order to let the department know what members of parliament think about certain situations. We realize that this is a department which is very difficult to administer, and I have said at almost every opportunity how grateful I am to the department for being so understanding from time to time, and I say now that we are getting some fast and considerate service.
I want to say a word of commendation also to the parliamentary secretary to the minister. Some weeks ago I brought a simple matter to his attention, a matter which required an immediate reply. I did not want to burden the officials or the minister with it, but I did trouble the parliamentary secretary and he gave attention to it very


promptly. I certainly want to express my gratitude for that. I feel that this is the time for it, and that it is also the time to be critical.
I can only underscore my sincere plea to the minister that she could do this country no better service than to see that the act is revised and made uniform; that it be consolidated, together with all the orders in council, in order that it may be not only a clear-cut statement of policy but also a clear guide to just who is and who is not admissible to this country. These things should not be left to orders in council or ministerial decisions or entirely to the discretion of the inquiry officer.
I know there must be some discretion given to these men and that they exercise it well, but such discretion is dangerous if one makes it final. We do not know what mood a particular official may be in. He may be distressed by domestic problems when he makes a decision. His decision has to be respected, but all I ask is that we do not allow it to be final as if it were a decision of the supreme court. We should allow facilities for review. It seems to me that when it is referred to a board of appeal this again is a departmental board, and there may be some concern for the position of an inquiry officer who is, after all, a colleague. There might be some uncontrollable influences involved of an intangible nature. If a man feels aggrieved and wants to take the matter to the courts he should be allowed to do so.
I urge the minister to take another look at section 39. I do not suggest that the bill standing in my name that seeks to amend section 39 is a panacea or cure-all, and I am prepared to withdraw it at any time or to agree to let the minister draft one in her own name or to convert and adapt mine and make it her own bill. I do not seek kudos for the bill. I am only eager to see that every immigrant, whether landed or not, is given justice and has his day in court. I think the act as it stands is in need of revision but would serve as an excellent foundation for a new act. If reviewed, amended and revised I do not think there would be an immigration act in the world capable of surpassing it.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps I could make a few general comments on the remarks, suggestions and criticisms of the hon. member for Cartier. First of all I should like to assure him that the decisions which are made in individual cases, to which he has referred, are not used as rulings by the department, simply because no two cases are ever exactly alike. It is true that from time to time people ask, "Why were

my relatives not admitted when this group are over here in exactly the same circumstances?" They are not in exactly the same circumstances. We find that time after time. So long as the minister is charged with exercising discretion then I must do that.
I agree with the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate that, if parliament wished to take away from the minister the discretionary power, it would certainly lighten my task very considerably. I would no longer be able to admit anyone by order in council. I am not sure that is what the hon. member for Cartier wants. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate just made a plea for more use of orders in council and the hon. member for Cartier says we should have less, that the act itself should stipulate who can or cannot enter the country and we should adhere rigidly to those classification. I am unable to agree with the hon. gentleman on that point. I believe there must be flexibility even though it makes the job of the minister more onerous.
The hon. member referred specifically to the statement I made in the house in August, 1958 and also to the one I made a few days ago with reference to fiancees. The very reason these statements were made in this chamber was to permit hon. members to comment on them, to disagree with them if they wish, and in neither case was there any noticeable disagreement.

But that is not the point I wanted to make. The point is that the house was informed of the changes. The information was brought forward and presented to hon. members for their approval or disapproval as the case may be. I think it could scarcely be expected that every change in the regulations and every administrative ruling should be submitted to parliament for debate. They would be held in abeyance for many months if that were done, and it would be tantamount to amending the regulations or the act as the case may be.
With respect to a revision of the act, I possibly have been guilty of some loose expressions referring to amendment when I
16,	1960	SOU
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration meant revision, or referring to revision when I meant amendment, but I hope hon. members will forgive me. What we do propose is a revision of the act. Quite apart from any alterations which may be made with respect to admissible groups we feel that the present act has probably had a few patches put on it here and there and is no longer as understandable a document as it might be. It is seven years old, as the hon. member has said, and I would hope to put it into a little more lucid form so there will not be the misunderstandings that have occurred in the past.
I can assure hon. members that as soon as the department and the government are ready with a revision of the act, ample opportunity will be given to all hon. members to voice their approval or disapproval and to make suggestions. It is my intention to make the draft act available not only to hon. members of the committee for their consideration but also to members of interested groups, including the voluntary agencies which work so closely with the department in the encouragement and care of new residents coming into Canada and also the various church groups, labour groups and others who are interested. I hope that all will have an opportunity to express their views.
I might say that the views expressed by these organizations in the past, sometimes in a formal way and sometimes by letters and resolutions, have been carefully considered and will continue to be given close attention regardless of the source from which they come. We do not pass lightly over or toss aside expressions of opinion; they are given careful consideration indeed. That may assist in explaining why the introduction of the revision has taken so long. I agree with the hon. member for Kootenay West that this is a matter that should not be hurried just for the sake of bringing in a new act, much as I should have liked to introduce it before now. I believe it is better to take time and make sure that the opinions of all have been carefully considered. In this way we will finally have a workable piece of legislation, one that will meet the approval of all groups of Canadians who have an interest in this department of government.
I had not intended to devote this time to answering specific questions that were raised, but I thought these few comments would be of interest to hon. members of the committee.

If before the end of this session the hon. lady could give first reading to her bill it seems to me this would be an admirable way to expedite its passage in another session. If it could be brought in with the understanding that it would get no more than first reading, so it would be published, then it seems to me there would be a good opportunity during the recess to have everyone interested look at it. Then when the new bill was introduced in another session, as was done with the Income Tax Act and innumerable statutes, a lot more progress would be made, because many of the representations would be known. I just offer that as a suggestion.
Since we met last week I have been thinking about something that I spoke about somewhat tentatively at that time, and that is this very awkward problem of dealing with visitors who have been ordered deported. I listened with the respect that I always accord to the hon. member for Cartier when he spoke this morning, because the hon. member has had perhaps as much experience with the problems of immigrants and would-be immigrants as any hon. member in this house. There is no member who is more genuinely


which were made upon me every year I was minister, that I was not bringing enough people into this country; that it was not being populated. When you look at the record, sir, you see what has happened.
I venture to say the indications are that immigration in the year 1960 will be no greater than it was in 1959, despite the Prime Minister's generous offer in London a short time ago that tens of thousands of immigrants would be welcomed to this country and there would be no trouble in finding jobs for them. I do say that I hope, before too many of the tens of thousands of job-seekers come to this country under any immigration policy, the minister will see that her colleague the Minister of Labour first tells those Canadians who are looking for jobs where the jobs are and gives them a chance to take them; because, as has been repeatedly pointed out from this side of the chamber, many of these job opportunities to which reference has been made are in categories that many a Canadian would be very happy to fill if he were given the opportunity.

When I was speaking the other day I said I thought that as long as we had the large scale unemployment which we unfortunately seem to be having now, in summer as well as winter, I did not think there should be any open placement immigration. I want to make that clear at once. The surest way to kill immigration altogether is to bring to this country by false advertising people who have no connection with it, and have them walk the streets for months looking for jobs, or have them lose a job or get a substandard job; then three months later they go home again and advertise what a poor country this is. The worst blow to desirable immigration in this country for years and years, in my opinion, was the way the Arrow contract was ended, with the consequences that had on our British immigration. The minister knows what I am talking about here.
But what I actually said was that this was so different from the advertisements. We were castigated over and over again. It was the Liberal view, and it is the Liberal view today, that immigration should be geared to the absorptive capacity of the country. We were told by the Minister of Justice and the Prime Minister that our immigration was far too low. In fact the Prime Minister got the figure up in the exuberance of the election campaign of 1957, less than six weeks before the government stopped all open placement immigration. He told a very select organization in Ontario that immigration should be 600,000 a year; at least that


is what it worked out to. He said an increase of 4 per cent a year. It was the extraordinary difference between what members of the Progressive Conservative opposition said on immigration and the practice since that I was drawing to the attention of the committee. The fact that I draw to the attention of the committee the contradictions of hon. members opposite does not mean that I share their views, because in most cases I do not.
The hon. lady said the immigration appeal board had not been established in 1955 when the criticism was made by the Prime Minister, and that is quite right. But I also point out to the hon. lady that of the cases to which the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice referred, I cannot remember one single case of a landed immigrant, although there may have been the odd one. I think they were all cases of persons who had never been accepted qs immigrants, which was the cause of this charge of lawlessness. I have never for one moment contested the fact that a person who was a landed immigrant had rights. I always said that; but no distinction was made, as the quotation I read from the Minister of Justice shows quite clearly.
It is true that the immigration appeal board now hears appeals by visitors, but I have no idea on what basis they do that, and I would be interested to hear the hon. lady tell us on what basis they hear those appeals. I do not mean that there is an order in council empowering them to do that, but I would like to know what criterion they use and how they go about it. It does not seem to me that there is any law upon which they can determine a case; they must merely act as a substitute or a screen for the minister.
I have no objection to that. I think the minister was very wise, and perhaps I might have saved myself a little agony if I had done that, too. But it seemed to me, and it seems to me still, that it was rather difficult to give a tribunal the capacity to decide something when it had no law on which to make the decision. In the case of a landed immigrant we know that the reason for deportation has to be precisely stated, under what section of the act it comes and what the circumstances are. But in the case of visitors all that is said is that they are not suitable, and that is all that under the law can be said unless you want to say that they are in one of the prohibited classes. I think the minister will agree, considering what the prohibited classes are, that that is casting a very severe reflection upon an applicant, and one would want to be sure one was right before making such reflections.
Therefore I would be interested to know on what basis the decisions are made and what criterion is used by the board in dealing

with the applications of visitors. It seems to me that is the only point that has not been dealt with by the minister which requires any further clarification.

Mr. Chairman, I just want to comment on this hocus-pocus of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. Here is a minister of immigration of a former government, in the dying days of the Liberal party, now dead. I would like to say that as far as the people of Canada are concerned they certainly appreciate the attitude of this government in doing away with hocus-pocus in the immigration department of the sort of which we had an example this afternoon. I can very well remember the present Prime Minister in the 1957 and 1958 election campaigns making it very clear that no country had more sympathy than Canada for people who wished to come here when it was not wise to bring people here for whom jobs were not available and while this country could not absorb them. Do not forget that they were the days of the Liberal party when unemployment was at a peak.
I suggest that if the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate had spent as much effort, when his government approved the St. Lawrence seaway, in getting them to approve and build the Chignecto canal, he would not be called a renegade in the maritime provinces today.

speechtext: My memory has been reinforced by an account of the Prime Minister's speech which I have before me from the Globe and Mail, Toronto, April 27, 1957.
