maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REQUEST FOR REPORT ON MEETING OF FISCAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
My honourable and distinguished friend from Bonavista-Twillingate has, I am afraid, covered the subject on which I had intended to speak. However, there is a situation which I should like to draw to the attention of the minister based upon the statement the hon. lady made in her opening remarks on June 9, as reported in Hansard of that date at page 4711. 1 quote:
A new policy governing temporary residents of Canada was announced in August, 1958 which made it possible to regularize the status of several thousands of persons who had previously entered the country on a non-immigrant basis.
This statement of policy seems to be in contradiction to the experience of a young woman who came to Canada on a visitor's visa and who, while she was here, met an eligible bachelor, a fine young man, who fell in love with her and proposed marriage. The first intimation I had of this romance came to me in a letter from Rev. L. Mulder, pastor of the Christian Reformed church, which I shall read for the information of the committee. It is addressed to me:
One of our eligible bachelors in our congregation has a problem, and after hearing about it I promised to write you about it.
Four months ago a girl came from Holland on a visitor's visa to visit relatives in the lakehead. She realized that she could not make the decision to stay here if she wanted to. Bachelor began to see the girl and they now have firm plans to get married next spring. The boy is about 30, the girl 25 years of age. They went to the immigration here to ask permission for the girl to stay here. No sir, law was law. Even if they were going to get married next spring-
This, by the way, was last August.
[DOT]-the girl first has to make the journey back to Holland and then immigrate properly. This involves extra money for nothing the couple argues, but to no avail, the immigration does not budge. Is there any appeal possible as far as you know, or is it better not to make any fuss and make a round trip to Holland?
Could you please let us know the best plan of campaign?
The young gent is not yet a Canadian citizen; does that make any difference?

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
I immediately took up this matter with the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. She in turn asked her private secretary to look into the matter. In due course I received a reply, which I am going to read; it is addressed to me:
This Is with reference to Miss Hoey's letter of September 9, 1959, concerning Miss Antje Bolt of Holland who desires to remain in Canada permanently.
According to a report received from the immigration officials in Fort William, this young lady entered Canada as a visitor on April 1, 1959. She has made inquiries regarding the possibility of being allowed to remain in Canada and the Fort William officials have explained the situation to her.
X would refer you to a statement made by my minister in the house on August 23, 1958, in connection with immigration procedure in dealing with non-immigrants. A person who applies at a visa office for temporary admission to Canada is required to sign a statement to the effect he understands he is being allowed to enter Canada on a temporary basis only and will effect departure from Canada on or before the expiration of the period of authorized temporary stay. He further signifies that he will not apply to remain in Canada permanently and that he understands failure to leave voluntarily in accordance with the undertaking renders him liable to deportation. May I point out that Miss Bolt signed the non-immigrant undertaking at the visa office in The Hague prior to coming to Canada.
It is the policy of this department to discourage non-immigrants who arrive in this country after August 31, 1958, from applying for landing. As a consequence it is, therefore, not possible to take favourable action on behalf of Miss Bolt. I can only suggest that on her return to Holland a formal application for her admission be filed by her fiance at the Fort William office or she make application on her own at The Hague office.
I realize that this advice comes as a disappointment to the parties concerned but I am sure you will understand the department would not be justified, in fairness to other cases, in making an exception in this particular instance.
That is where the matter ended. I deplore very much indeed this lack of appreciation for love and romance on the part of some members of the department who should have given special consideration to this case at once, particularly as the department is presided over by a charming lady such as we have in the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. Leaving the spirit of romance aside, the very principle enunciated by the minister in the statement which I read a minute ago, if it is a statement which has any validity at all, should certainly have applied to this girl.
I should like a statement from the minister with regard to this particular case and similar cases, of which there must be a considerable number in the country. It appears to me that when a couple meet in Canada and one of the parties concerned is only here on a temporary basis, he or she should be considered for permanent admission. They should be allowed to get married and have children and populate the country, which would be far

more desirable in the long run; that is, to have many children to populate the country as we want it to be populated.
The minister has already indicated that amendments to the act will not be forthcoming during this session. I do not fully agree with all the statements made by my distinguished colleague, the former minister of citizenship and immigration, though I have great respect for his good judgment. There are also certain aspects of the statements which were made by the late Mr. Mackenzie King about which I have some reservations. I would not wish to enter into that matter now, because I am waiting for the government to bring in the amendments to the Immigration Act. That will be the appropriate time for me and others to enter into a discussion of what will be best for Canada.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REQUEST FOR REPORT ON MEETING OF FISCAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to set the hon. member's mind at rest. I can assure him that the course of true love is constantly being smoothed for a great many couples by this department. I do not know the extension of stay; perhaps it was for a year or more. We usually have young people say they intend to marry and they give a specific period of time, say three or four months or something like that. We extend the visit to take care of that intention, and then if the young couple marry we of course would not separate husband and wife. We would certainly land the new spouse. But that is not always the case. Many young people say they have fallen in love and intend to marry, but then when landed they decide the love was not quite as true as they thought. I recall one case in which one man managed to bring in seven or eight different fiancees, until the department finally decided that this was scarcely a true indication of his intentions.
I can assure the hon. member that although all these cases have to be viewed on an individual basis, we do what we can to assist them. I do not know what the final outcome of this particular case was, whether or not the young lady went back to Holland. If she had given a definite or even an approximate date which had not been too far in the future, and had asked for an extension, she certainly would have been given an extension of her visitor's visa.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REQUEST FOR REPORT ON MEETING OF FISCAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Will the minister allow me one question? Has there been a case of a couple marrying prior to asking permission to remain, and have they received that permission?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REQUEST FOR REPORT ON MEETING OF FISCAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The young lady would
have to undergo health examinations, of course. This opens up a field with very broad ramifications. We do not separate families. Even if she had not complied strictly with
the immigration regulations we would have advised her as to how she should conduct herself in order to remain in Canada with her husband.
In other words, what is required is to prove your matrimonial intentions.

I have three or four questions I should like to ask at once, and then the minister could answer them all. I do not intend to make any more speeches, but I should like to bring to the minister's attention a case that has interested me. I do not like to enter into a discussion of individual cases, and unless the minister wants me to I will not mention the name in this file. I know the minister has received many representations with respect to this case. The only ground on which the case was turned down was that the person being applied for was a half sister instead of a full sister of the person applying. I do not know what the legal advisers of the department would say about whether a half sister is a sister within the meaning of the regulations.
I know what I would have done with this case if it had not been within the regulations. I would have submitted it to the governor in council for approval on the basis of the facts I have. I admit that it is not always possible to have all the facts in these cases. There may be some other reason that has not been given. On the face of it, and based on such information as I have available to me, this person was otherwise eligible except for this particular circumstance. The person had come here as a visitor, as people sometimes do from countries behind the iron curtain because it is easier to come as a visitor than as a immigrant, and subsequently wished to change status. This happened after that regrettable administrative decision of 1958.
I think the minister made an awful mistake when she said earlier, especially in my hearing, that because I categorically objected only once to that statement of policy in 1958 there was very little opposition to it. If I have to repeat my objections one hundred times in order to convince the minister that I am utterly opposed to it I shall attempt to do so, but I hope she will take it that I have repeated my objection a hundred times.
Oh, I am convinced.

I think that regulation which forces people who are already in this country to go home and then apply-the people being otherwise eligible-is stupid and inhuman and should not be carried on one day longer. If I can make my views on that subject any more emphatic I should like to do so. I think that in marginal cases like the one I am referring to now, of a
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration half sister, if that is the only objection it should not be considered an objection at all in sponsored cases.

It is not, either, Mr. Chairman. We have made no difference at all between half sisters and sisters. If the person were otherwise admissible the fact that she was a half sister would not bar her from entry to the country. If she has been refused entry I should think there would have been other circumstances.
I do not intend to go over the file here in the committee, because in my opinion that would be an abuse. I will let the minister have another look at it privately.
We definitely do let in half sisters the same as sisters.

I have another question to pursue. I asked the Prime Minister one day just at the time the Prime Minister of Japan was here whether there had been any discussion about a revival of the gentleman's agreement, or any change in the conditions of admission of would-be Japanese immigrants. The minister perhaps saw or had drawn to her attention a letter written by the Japanese ambassador which appeared in the New Canadian of February 6, 1960. I referred to that in the house at the time. The Japanese ambassador said in his letter:
During the recent visit to Ottawa of Prime Minister Kishi, the question of immigration was discussed with Canadian government leaders.
In dealing with the matter in the house the Prime Minister stated, as reported at page 258 of Hansard of January 25, 1960:
I speak from memory but X do not think there was any consideration given or any discussion of that subject.
I should point out that I was being much more specific on that occasion. I referred then to the pre-war agreement. We also know there was some talk about admitting some Japanese to the province of Saskatchewan to aid in the establishment of an industry there. If there is anything new at all about immigration from Japan I think the minister should tell us about it.
The hon. lady should also tell us whether there have been any developments with respect to the admission of immigrants from the British West Indies. The minister will recall that I said on one or two occasions, both when I was minister and since, that it would have been my intention, had I remained in the government, to recommend to my colleagues the establishment of a regime for the British West Indies similar to that which exists in respect to India, Pakistan and Ceylon; namely, to establish some kind of quota by agreement with the federation.
5020	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
I did not think that was practical before the federation was founded. As a matter of fact I had a secret aspiration to go there as a representative of the Canadian government on the occasion the federation was established, but it was another minister of citizenship and immigration who went instead. I would have hoped that this visit would melt the heart of the hon. lady and make her realize that an improved regime should be introduced which would meet this peculiarly difficult situation. It is a difficult situation, and I do not pretend it is not.
I wish also to make a request of the government concerning the residual health and welfare care of refugees who are privately sponsored. I still think that if in this world refugee year we are to play a part at all commensurate with the capacity of this country, the present serious difficulty should be overcome and could be overcome by the government at very little cost to the Canadian taxpayers.
There is one other matter I do want to bring to the minister's attention. The minister may know something about the Canadian-British education committee. I do not know whether she does. If she does not, I do know that some of her officials know something about it. This is an organization which exists in London for the purpose of promoting the attendance at Canadian universities of school boys, matriculants, from the schools of the United Kingdom. It is not an immigration scheme at all; but it does seem to me that it might well be worth the while of the government to look into this scheme and see whether the residual value of assisting this committee in its activities might not be productive of a very good kind of immigrant who is otherwise very hard to get. I do not want to take up the time of the committee. I just wanted to mention it so there would be a reference to it in Hansard and I should be glad to show the correspondence to the minister.

I thank the hon. member for his suggestions. I do not know precisely what the reason is but, of course, we do not have an immigration office in Japan; also, we do not have a great many applications for entry. In 1959, 191 Japanese came into Canada. That is not a very great number; it is the highest of any year since the war. It has been creeping up. The years 1957, 1958 and 1959 are all pretty much on a par, and in 1957 there was an increase, and the number was nearly double what it had been the year before; there were 178 in 1957; 188 in 1958; and 191 in 1959. When we have requests for special cases, of course, we do our best to co-operate. The Saskatchewan situation is an example.
Has anything been done about it?

Yes; it is being worked on. Arrangements are being carried forward through the department with respect to whatever establishment is required to set up the industry described. I do not think I can go farther than that because I cannot give details.
With regard to the West Indies there is, of course, a quota but not on the same basis as that for India, Pakistan and Ceylon. It is a quota of domestics and the quota was established, as the hon. member knows, after consultation with the government of the West Indies, based largely on the capacity of the West Indies government to train those domestics. Prior to federation two or three of the islands had quotas allotted to them. After federation representations were made by the West Indies minister responsible for an increase in the number and the number was increased by 50, so that at the present time there are 250 from the West Indies proper and 30 from British Guiana. My understanding is that this is pretty much all they can train in a year. They might squeeze in a few more. These people go to training schools and come here supposedly as properly trained domestics, having regard to the work which they will be required to do while in Canada.
However, in addition to those domestics who come forward, there are a certain number of specially qualified persons who come in simply because they have qualifications which are of value to Canada. These would include in some instances students who had come up here to pursue higher education and who, upon completion of their education, would apply to remain because they would have no difficulty whatsoever in securing employment. In fact, sometimes employment is offered to them because of their particular qualities and capabilities. Some of those people come in and then, of course, any person who is in the country may apply for his or her relatives, and some of those come in, with the result that over the last two years approximately 1,200 people have come in from the British West Indies. There again the number has grown over the years, and those two years are the highest of any years. I think this is a general explanation.

May I say just a word about this. I understand that the West Indies situation represents a quota within a quota, a quota in numbers which is qualified by limitation to a certain occupation, namely domestic service, and that the governments of the

West Indies take responsibility for the training and certifying as to the training of those who come here?
That is correct.

The Canadian government authorities take no responsibility for that. When they come here I take it they are supposed to be engaged in domestic service. Does the department have any record as to how long they stay in domestic service, how many of them leave domestic service, and if they do leave domestic service, is there any intervention on the part of the authorities to try to persuade them to go back to the occupation which they undertook to follow when they came into the country?

No, Mr. Chairman; we do not follow them up unless they come back to us and ask for employment; unless their employment terminates we would not have any record of them. We do not follow any of the immigrants once they are in the country. In so far as their placements is concernd, we turn them over to the national employment service and placement is made through that service.

I have just one question on this item. Can the minister inform the committee what percentage of the loans which were given to assist passages is uncollected, and if there is any difficulty in collecting from any particular group? I have been informed by the officials that they are behind in some cases.

I can get that information for the hon. member. Since the scheme first went into operation on February 1, 1951, there have been 75,559 loans for a total of $19,127,558, of which $15 million odd has been collected. This does not indicate that the remainder are all delinquents. Repayments are being made all the time. I can find out for the hon. member what the amount is that we consider to be bad debts. I presume that is what he wants to know.
Yes.
I will get that information.

Can the minister tell the committee whether the Canadian immigration centre on St. Antoine street in Montreal has been closed? If it has been closed, were the employees there integrated into some other department?

This was discussed in the house some time ago, Mr. Chairman. The hall was closed. It was an unsatisfactory
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration place and there had been a great many complaints about it. Finally, it was closed. We tried to place the employees wherever we could. Some of them, very few of them, did not want to be placed. Some of them were transferred to Quebec. Those who did not wish to go to Quebec-we consulted with the national employment service-in some instances we had them transferred to other departments of government. I do not know whether I can give the hon. member the exact number. Nine of them were re-assigned either in this department or in two other departments; two of them retired and the rest of them were taken care of either in Quebec or in some other employment.

Just before the item carries I should like to say to the minister that I think it would be a good idea if the government would give consideration to establishing a quota for the West Indies without an occupational limitation. The occupational limitation was only established very reluctantly by the previous government in the first place. I can speak about this because I do not think there was anything I did as minister that I did more reluctantly. It was done not because anyone in Canada was asking for it but because of representations received in the first instance from the government of Jamaica. I am not suggesting any large scale immigration. I do not think the West Indian community in Canada or anyone else really wants to see mass immigration. I do think that if we could have a quota such as the Indian quota-I do not mean in numbers because I have no suggestion as to numbers-which would include any kind of occupation and did not impose an occupational limitation it would be more consonant with the dignity of the new federation and would make for better relations.

I cannot speak from statistics at the moment but my impression is that a reasonable number come in now under the situation as I have described it. I know that persons who come to me and complain about the lack of immigration from the West Indies are always amazed when I tell them how many have actually come to Canada. I remember having one gentleman in my office about six months ago who complained very bitterly and said that he thought there should be a quota, as the hon. member has said, over and above the domestic quota. I said, "How many do you think should be allowed to come in from the West Indies in any one year"? He said, "Oh, I would think possibly 500 in addition to the domestic quota". I said, "That would be 750". He said, "Yes". I said, "Well, 1,200 came in". He was amazed. He said, "That is not true; that could not

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration possibly be true". I said, "It is true". I had great difficulty in convincing him that was a fact. I think there is a great deal of misinformation abroad. People do not realize that there is actually not a large but a very steady flow. There might be something to be said for some different arrangement, but I can assure the hon. member that we are watching this situation all the time.

I should not like any misunderstanding to arise. I would not suggest for one minute that there should be a quota as a substitute for close relative sponsorship. I regard close relative sponsorship as the best means of immigration there is, and I think that our experience since the war has shown us that it is. But it did seem to me that in addition a small quota that was not restricted as to occupation might perhaps be symbolic in the same way as the Indian, Pakistan and Ceylon quotas if the government of the West Indies wanted it. Of course, if they do not want it it would serve no purpose whatever.
This is a very interesting point because generally speaking I do not like quotas.
Nor do I.

In the case of Ceylon and Pakistan they have not taken up their quotas at any time although they exist. In the case of India we made arrangements a year ago that each quota number would apply to a family unit instead of to an individual, which eased matters considerably in that regard. The quota was also split 50-50, I believe, between open placements and relatives. As a result of making relatives or family units half of the quota instead of an individual quota I think the situation is in fair shape there. If we did the same thing for the West Indies I would think that in the long run we would probably wind up with just about what we have today.

That could well be. I am not pressing this unduly. I though it might remove a sense of grievance. I should like to say this right now to the hon. lady so that there will be no misunderstanding. If there is any suggestion by the government of Japan that they would like to have the prewar gentlemen's agreement revived I would hope the government would welcome that suggestion.

Mr. Chairman, there are difficulties with respect to quotas and, as the minister knows, in principle it is certainly not the best way to deal with immigration. As I recall, the value of the quota as applied to Pakistan, India and Ceylon was not so


much in the number that came under the quota but that it removed a feeling of discrimination which had existed before because it put Canadians going into those countries on the same basis as nationals of those countries coming into Canada. So they no longer had a feeling of discrimination. If the same principle could be applied to the federation of the West Indies, and if the government there felt that there was a kind of discrimination against them, it might be useful from that point of view.

Item agreed to.
505. Administration of the Immigration Act- further amount required, $25,000.
Perhaps the hon. lady would tell us why she needs more money when immigration is going down.
Increasing costs arising mostly from increases in salaries.

speechtext: What is the situation in Hong Kong with relation to departmental employees and those hired on a casual basis?

Trans-oceanic and inland transportation and other assistance for immigrants and settlers, subject to the approval of treasury board, including care en route and while awaiting employment; and payments to the provinces pursuant to agreements entered into, with the approval of the governor in council, in respect of expenses incurred by the provinces for indigent immigrants, $2,100,000.

Has the hon. lady figures up to the latest available date as to the amount paid out by way of assistance to immigrants and the number of persons who have benefited therefrom? I do not mean family assistance.
You mean welfare assistance?
Welfare assistance.
In 1959-60 the amount for food and shelter was $92,196.35, about one tenth of the amount for 1958-59 which was $986,000 odd. In 1957-58 the amount was $5,732,000.
But in that year it included transportation as well.
That could be.
It included transportation of the Hungarians.
That is probably quite right. Is the hon. member interested in family assistance?
Family assistance is just family allowances under another name.

I cannot give the hon. member the total number of persons assisted because it varies from month to month. In 1959 the minimum number was 251 in November and the maximum number was 1,282 in January. That gives a general picture.
That included dependants as well?
Yes.
Can the hon. lady say whether very many of the Hungarian refugees are now receiving assistance from the department?

I think I can say no to
that. These reports were coming in regularly but of late the figures have dwindled to the point where it was scarcely worth reporting any more. I do not have a specific report on the matter. If the hon. member is interested I can secure the information.

I should like to have it put on the record at some stage because, speaking personally, I take great pride in the fact that we brought to this country- the present government continued what we started-37,000 of these Hungarian refugees who had nothing but the clothes on their backs and practically all of them have established themselves in this country and are earning their own living today.

This is really just an amplification of what I said. In January, 1959, which is a year and a half ago, there were 349 Hungarian refugees receiving assistance. My officials tell me that since that time the number has dwindled to such a point that we no longer keep track of them.
I am very glad to hear that.

47. Citizenship registration branch, $716,892.
I should like to ask the hon. lady if she has a statement she would like to make on this branch.

I have a few short remarks. During the calendar year 1959 the number of applications for Canadian citizenship were lower than for the preceding year. The number of persons acquiring Canadian citizenship dropped from 84,000 in 1958 to
71,000	in 1959. There was a similar drop in the number of Canadian citizens who applied for certificates of proof of citizenship. This number dropped from 49,000 in 1958 to 44,000 in 1959. During the year 1959 one new Canadian citizenship court was established in Hamilton, Ontario. In the current calendar year, one new court of Canadian citizenship, located at London, Ontario, has already been opened and additional courts of Canadian citizenship will be opened in Winnipeg, Edmonton, Vancouver and we hope in Moncton, New Brunswick. These new courts will bring to eight the total number of citizenship courts in operation.
I might add that while I know a good many of the county court judges who handled these applications in the past have been wonderful court judges and have taken a great interest in the applicants, I still feel that a uniform system is desirable. I hope that the day will come when most of our applicants for Canadian citizenship will go through our own departmental courts and not be forced to make their applications in courts which are primarily set up for the purpose of dealing with criminal and civil cases.

In so far as the courts are concerned, I must say that I cannot forbear doing a little boasting. I was responsible for the establishment of the first two courts in Toronto and Montreal. I took a great deal of satisfaction from the fact that these courts cost the taxpayers nothing. I think not only do they cost the taxpayers nothing but they provide such an infinitely better-I use the word "infinitely" almost in its correct etymological sense-service, a service so much better that there was no comparison. I would be interested in knowing something about the economics of the two new courts, perhaps the Hamilton one is the only one upon which the minister would have statistics. Is the Hamilton court costing the taxpayers something or is it paying for itself?

It was only started last year, so has just had about six months operation. However, even so, it reported a net revenue of $2,280.

I could, but not in its
entirety because the Hamilton court has not been operating for a full year. I really do not have a proper comparison.

I should like to take a minute or two to mention a couple of things. In the first place, I wonder if the minister thinks that the decline in the number of applicants is something that can be explained by a decline five years earlier-I would have to do a little arithmetic myself to see whether it would be-in the number of immigrants that year? I am wondering if it is following some pattern or if there is some other reason why the number has fallen off. I would be interested also in knowing whether there has been any improvement in the number of applications from British subjects for citizenship. I think the experience of the department was that the number was not as large in relation to other applicants, perhaps because they felt citizenship did not confer quite as great an advantage upon them as it did upon others. Some of us were rather disappointed that the number was not larger.
I would be interested to know also if the minister can tell us something about what promotional activities the department is carrying on with a view to urging people to make their applications promptly, and to bring before them the advantages of citizenship. Having listened to the hon. member for Fort William speak the last time the estimates were before the committee concerning the requirement of a knowledge of the English or French languages, I would say that on the first occasion when the citizenship act may again be before parliament for some reason-I would not go so far as to say we ought to make a special amendment for this purpose only-some clarification of the language should be made to indicate that some discretion should be shown by judges in connection with this matter. I was asked five years ago by someone in the committee on estimates what I thought would be an adequate knowledge of the English or French languages in the case of an applicant. I said if the applicant were someone who was employed, particularly if he was employed driving a motor car, I thought he ought to be able to read and speak pretty well. On


the other hand, if the applicant was a housewife who had several young children to bring up and very little time for much association with other people in the community or an older person who would not be in the employment stream, I thought if they could say "God Save the Queen"-maybe it was the king then-I would regard that as a fairly adequate knowledge.
I think it is desirable that citizens generally know the languages of the country. Some of the members of the treasury benches, knowing something of the difficulty even of learning one of the languages of their own country and also some of the advantages of doing so, would perhaps be more sympathetic now than they might have been at an earlier time toward some of these applicants. It seems to me some of these judges have been unduly conscientious, if I might perhaps use that word, about this requirement. Perhaps we should seek the next time the act is amended to do something to make that point clear. I agree completely with the hon. member for Fort William, who brought this matter before us the other day, that the last thing we want to do is to deny the mothers of families who have brought up good Canadian citizens many of them born in this country, citizenship simply because they have not had the time or the facility to learn to speak one of the official languages as well as the judges of the county courts speak it. I do want very warmly indeed to second what was so ably said the other day by the hon. member for Fort William.

As the hon. member knows we have a much better chance of making these suggestions to the presidents of our courts under the department than to the judges who, after all, are all-powerful in their own particular courts. While the minister might have some discretion if a case is approved by a judge, she has none whatever if the case is turned down by a judge. So so far as that is concerned I have no control over it, but I do think that as these courts are set up the situation will be improved.
I also think that through the advent of television more and more people will acquire a reasonable working knowledge of one of our two languages in Canada than possibly they did heretofore, because it is much easier to follow the television where action is joined with words than to follow radio where they only hear the sound. I think television is a great teacher for new people coming in.
I cannot give the hon. member any figures for 1959, but those persons from commonwealth countries who applied for citizenship

in 1957 numbered 8,650. This had increased to 10,235 in 1958 and I would think there is a similar increase for 1959.
Notwithstanding the general decline.

Yes. We have been promoting this. There is a new poster which is displayed in post offices and other public places in all parts of Canada which urges people to apply for citizenship. It particularly draws attention to the fact that British subjects should apply for Canadian citizenship. We have advertisements in the ethnic press, and generally speaking promotion is going on all the time. Our liaison officers in various parts of the country also do their part.
Just parenthetically may I say to the hon. lady that I do not think advertisements in the ethnic press would draw many British subjects to them.
No, I did not relate them to British subjects. I meant that that was one of our promotional activities.

48. Citizenship branch, $785,159.
Has the hon. lady anything to say about this vote?

Yes, I have. For the past two years the citizenship branch has been taking advantage of a reduced immigration flow to shift its attention from the more immediate problems of reception to those of social adjustment. More particularly this year efforts have been concentrated on language instruction and on integration at the neighbourhood level.
In the field of language classes, intensified liaison and promotional work with school authorities and throughout the immigrant population kept the national enrolment at close to 50,000, only slightly below previous levels. Teaching costs and free textbook distribution for beginners went down by less than 3.5 per cent. At the same time greater attention than ever was being paid to meeting special needs such as continued instruction throughout the summer, day courses for housewives, shift workers and hospital patients, and crash programs for immigrants awaiting placement. A gratifying measure of co-operation was secured from educational authorities in these fields throughout the vast majority of metropolitan centres. Finally, in addition to assisting in the conduct of a five regional week-end course for teachers of immigrants, the branch has been able to organize, with the co-operation of all provinces having a substantial immigrant population, a national six-week summer course for teachers at Toronto. The

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration purpose of this training is to build up a core of skilful teachers and supervisors which would ensure that the teaching of English or French to immigrants is conducted by the most efficient methods.
At the neighbourhood level the branch has redoubled its efforts to bring about early acceptance and integration of newcomers. With the help of a special film produced in several languages a national program with home and school and parent-teacher associations was initiated to interpret the educational problems of immigrant children to Canadians and to encourage immigrant participation in community action. Significant progress was also made in drawing immigrants into the membership of community centres, scouts and guides, women's institutes, credit unions, junior chambers of commerce, and in securing immigrant representation on boards of community agencies. At the same time the branch has encouraged and assisted local radio, television or press representatives in the production of feature series on the lives and contributions of immigrants.
Throughout world refugee year the liaison officers of the branch have contributed their services to the organization and activities of committees, both at the national and local levels.
In March, 1960 the citizenship branch completed a long awaited revision of several monographs of ethnic groups published under the title of "Notes on the Canadian family tree". This publication is now on sale at the Queen's printer.
A growing emphasis has been placed by the branch on the fostering of sound community attitudes among the younger generation. Last year the branch promoted an increased number of leadership training courses for young adults from various religious, racial and ethnic backgrounds. It continued to encourage wider community participation in observances of brotherhood and citizenship weeks. Furthermore, considerably more attention is being paid this year to the organization of appropriate festivities for Dominion day in various Canadian centres, and I might say notably here in Ottawa. The branch has also been very closely associated with advance plans for Canada's centenary both among voluntary organizations and at the government level.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Can the minister tell us what the cost is and how you would go about getting these certificates.
Any of our courts will supply an application form. The applicant is required to have the form completed and two passport type photographs sent along with it. The fee is $2.
Do these certificates pay for themselves?
I am sure they do in human satisfaction.

I find that mine which was signed by myself was very useful, but I wondered if the $2 covered the cost. I would think it did quite adequately, but I do not know whether the department has any statistics.

I hesitate to mention this. I do not want to be accused of making a great profit, but I understand that in 1954 the cost was 49 cents. Now, of course, it will be a little more than that, but I can assure the hon. member that they still pay for themselves.

I am very pleased to hear that because I certainly think they are worth the $2 which they cost. I never go out without mine and I have found it very useful on a good many occasions and I know a lot of other people who have too.
I just wanted to make one or two general observations with respect to the citizenship branch. I think the time has come when the minister should give very serious consideration to the amalgamation of the citizenship registration branch and the citizenship branch. It seems to me that with the establishment more generally across Canada of citizenship courts there could be a very much closer co-ordination, although I know there is a good deal of co-ordination already, there would be a more thorough focusing of attention upon immigrants and would-be citizens if the two branches were combined.
I do not say that should be done immediately, but I do think that very serious thought should be given, as far as possible, to reducing overhead and head office expenses and that sort of expense. In many cases I think it would be found that the functions of the two branches are so closely connected that there might well be, perhaps at a time when some changes in personnel are to be made anyway, consideration given to amalgamation.

I should also like to say a word or two about the publications of the citizenship branch. If I say anything which seems to be a little critical it would be very easy for the minister to say, "Why didn't you do something about it when you were there?" I suggested to the minister last year, and I think she has taken my advice to some limited extent, that we ought to put a value on many of these publications of a more general character. I am not referring so much to those specifically directed to the language instruction of immigrants because I am heartily in favour of that as long as it is done efficiently. But I do think that if perhaps some of these other publications were put to the acid test of price we might find we could make some savings to the treasury which I am sure would be welcome to the Minister of Finance and to the taxpayers. I know that of the total cost of the government of Canada the amount spent on the citizenship branch is small, but that applies to a great many other departments, and unless we apply economies wherever we can the cost of government will keep growing and growing.
I feel about a lot of government publications that if there were any way of getting them stopped it would be a wonderful thing, at least for members of parliament, and when it gets to the point that you have to spend much of your time every day moving them from one side of your desk to the other and, if one is conscientious, thinking you should be reading these things, one begins to wonder whether there is not some way of saving not only the taxpayers money but all the energy and the time of many other people in the country.
I do not intend to say anything about any of the publications specifically, but I do think this is one area where a good deal of thought might be given to co-ordination and amalgamation as a goal, and not too distant a goal either, in order to bring about a reduction in cost.

I am pleased to hear the hon. member speak in that vein because I feel much the same myself. As a matter of fact this year we have cut our appropriation from $53,725 to $21,600 and the number of publications we are putting out this year has been reduced. Some of the more popular ones will have to be reprinted; ones which I am sure the hon. gentleman would think very useful. Nevertheless, this year we are only reprinting ten publications.

I should just like to pose one question to the minister. This is something to which critical reference has been made from time to time, and perhaps some action is afoot to correct it, or perhaps it has been

corrected already. I make reference to the variation in approach used by various judges in dealing with applications for citizenship.
From my limited knowledge I understand that one judge may be strict, for argument sake, in his manner of questioning of applicants and in the type of questions and the degree of proficiency with which he wants those questions answered, compared with another judge who might be, for argument sake, more lenient. In fact the situation has been established, in some cases, where some areas of a province or some provinces become known as easy places for a person to pass the test of citizenship in so far as the questions asked are concerned compared with another country or another place in the province.
I wonder what consideration has been given to attempting to develop some unified approach that judges would follow in asking questions of applicants for citizenship in order that there can be a fairly uniform approach to this question across the country rather than having it vary from province to province or from county to county within the same province.

I think I have discussed that point with the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate when I was speaking. We really do not have any control over county court judges. That is one of the main reasons we would like to set up our own courts, because then we could suggest uniform procedures. I agree with the hon. member that it would be definitely advisable to have uniform procedures wherever they could be obtained.

I must apologize for not being here when this matter was being discussed earlier. However, it is not a question of attempting to control the county court judges and suggesting to them that they must ask certain questions or things of that nature. This arises out of a discussion I had with Judge Schultz in the county of Prince Rupert. He is a judge appointed during the last couple of years and he, as well as the citizenship council in Prince Rupert, believe that perhaps the proper procedure might be to have a list of types of questions which judges might use to advantage in obtaining information so as to ensure a greater degree of uniformity across the country.
We had some such scheme for a while, but it was not very popular with the judges.

On this first item of Indian affairs I think it would be appropriate for me to tell the committee something about the trip I made through western Canada last summer when it was my fortunate experience to come into personal touch with a considerable cross-section of our Indian population. I travelled some ten thousand miles, meeting Indians from 53 bands representative of over 220 reserves. From Island Lake in Manitoba to the coast of British Columbia I visited Indian families in their homes, discussed problems with band chiefs and councillors and saw the people at work in their many and varied occupations. Everywhere my attention was drawn to Indian schools, houses, community halls and other facilities on reserves.
Throughout the country I found a common interest by Indians in improved housing, advancement in education, community development and economic prosperity. Band chiefs and councillors are as one in their willingness to participate more fully in the administration of band affairs. From all bands I experienced a forthright, friendly reception which is characteristic of the human warmth of our Indian people. With these attributes they are going forward rapidly in their successful adjustment to the Canadian social and economic environment. It is indeed a privilege to work with them.
As already mentioned, Indian band councils are taking an increasing interest in the administration of band affairs. Approximately two thirds of all bands are now under the elective system and I am pleased to note that during the fiscal year just ended a number of Indian women were successful candidates in band elections, bringing to a total of six the number of Indian women holding the office of chief and 73 as councillors, 10 of whom were elected under the tribal custom.
The 1960-61 main estimates for Indian affairs show an increase of $3,581,296 over 1959-60. The major portion of this increase is attributable to two basic important fields, namely education and welfare.
I feel that too much emphasis cannot be placed on our educational program, for it is only through the processes of education that we can enable our Indian people, on their own initiative and resources, to advance to higher economic and social levels. To further emphasize this point I would state that of the total appropriation for Indian affairs, 59.8 per cent will be used for educational purposes.
Again this year there has been a very marked increase in the number of Indian pupils receiving an education. For the 195960 fiscal year the figures show a total enrolment of 40,637 pupils of whom 9,479 are enrolled at non-Indian schools, universities,
5028	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration teachers' colleges and commercial and trade schools. This latter figure represents an increase of nearly 1,300 over last year. Particularly encouraging is the increase in the number of students enrolled at the university level which has now reached 58 including those enrolled in grade 13.
In recent years a program of organizing education committees composed of Indian band members was introduced to deal with school matters on the reserves. It is hoped that these will become embryonic school boards and in this way give to the Indian people an element of control and direction in the field of education which should be of vital concern to them. I am pleased to report that the number of these committees now stands at 19, an increase of 6 over the previous fiscal year.
Each year there has been an interest expressed in the scholarship program of the department and during the 1959-60 fiscal year 17 scholarship awards were made to outstanding Indian students. This represents an expenditure of $14,375 for this purpose.
It is proposed to construct during the fiscal year 118 classrooms together with other necessary construction and including 74 staff residences at an estimated total cost of $7,362,500 which includes all necessary equipment, and provision has been made for substantial contributions toward construction of provincial schools which would enable the joint education of Indian and non-Indian children. Both the Indian day and residential school programs have been maintained at the same level.
There has been a steady development of adult education programs designed primarily to attack the problem of illiteracy which is to be found on many of the reserves. During the 1958-59 fiscal year this program served 857 students but the numbers have increased for the 1959-60 year. The returns show a total enrolment of 1,223 with the greatest numbers enrolled in literacy and homemaking courses.
During the last fiscal year a record total of 1,465 houses were built on Indian reserves and in Indian communities across Canada and another 228 units were started. This is a larger number of houses than has been built in any previous year. The achievement is particularly noteworthy since standards have been steadily improved and the costs of material and labour have continued to increase. These houses were financed from the $2 million in public funds in the 1959-60 estimates and the contribution from the Indians themselves in the form of labour, cash, materials, band funds and V.L.A. grants. I should like to pay particular tribute to the increased measure of responsibility being assumed by individual Indians and band


councils who, through their co-operation and participation, have made this achievement possible.
It is proposed to maintain the same rate of expenditure for Indian housing in 1960-61. There will be increased emphasis on better standards of construction, improved sanitary facilities and adequate community planning. Every effort will be made to encourage greater participation of the prospective Indian home owner in the planning, financing and construction of his house. Special attention will be given to the needs of Indians in northern and remote areas in order to bring housing in such Indian communities up to an acceptable standard as soon as possible.
It will be noted that there is an increase in operating costs for welfare of $1,375,313. When presenting the estimates for 1959-60 I mentioned the introduction of revised methods and improved standards of relief administration on behalf of Indians. It is a pleasure to report that these methods and the new rates which went into effect April 1, 1959 have proved to be generally satisfactory. Indians, on the whole, have responded splendidly to the responsibility which the management of this income placed in their hands under the new procedures. They have fully justified our confidence in their ability to do so. Indigent members of 20 per cent of the bands in Canada now receive relief assistance in cash and it is planned to extend this practice to additional bands this year.
I should like to make it clear that the scales of assistance established are for food only. In addition, assistance is granted, as necessary, in individual cases for such purposes as fuel, clothing, necessary household equipment and shelter. I should like to stress that the assistance granted is subject to a means test.
It is an important objective of my department to make it possible for Indians to have access to the same sources of assistance in time of need as other persons in the province in which they live. I announced to the house on April 8 last that the federal government is prepared to negotiate agreements with the governments of the various provinces for the extension of the normal provincial services to persons residing on Indian reserves. The purpose is to avoid the development of exclusive welfare services on reserves which would tend to set Indians apart from other Canadians and would duplicate existing provincial programs in adjacent nonIndian communities. I said that in negotiating these agreements the federal government is prepared to pay a reasonable share of the cost of the benefits over and above the

federal contribution under existing federal-provincial agreements such as the Unemployment Assistance Act. In addition, this government is prepared to share with provinces reasonable costs of additional staff and of administration required. In cases where provincial welfare programs are normally administered by municipalities, my department will be prepared to negotiate agreements which will enable bands to fulfil the same functions and discharge the same responsibilities.
I also announced on April 8 that in future my department will undertake to provide essential welfare services on behalf of certain categories of non-Indians on reserves. The principal concern is for women of Indian origin who have lost Indian status through enfranchisement or marriage but who have no alternative but to return to friends and relatives on the reserves. The decision to implement this policy was based on humanitarian considerations. Essential assistance to these people when in need can now be provided in the same manner and to the same extent as for persons of Indian status on the reserves in similar circumstances.
Last year I informed you of the establishment of a new division, one of the prime functions of which is to promote the employment of Indians. Placement officers are now functioning in the eight administrative regions. From the inception of the placement program in April, 1957 approximately 500 individuals have been established in permanent employment and 4,000 in rural and seasonal occupations. Almost half of these placements were made during the fiscal year just ended.
One hundred revolving fund loans in the total amount of $109,209.78 were approved during the last fiscal year to assist Indians to become established. While a higher proportion of this amount was used to develop the agriculture industry, the department also supplied repayable advances to enable Indians to purchase seed, farming equipment and other supplies. A number of foundation livestock herds were made available to Indians in the prairie provinces. The increase in the item for equipment and supplies will make possible the continuation and further expansion of this program.
In continuation of the accelerated forestry inventory program initiated two years ago in British Columbia arrangements have been made with the forestry branch of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources to carry out forest surveys on all forested Indian reserves east of the Rockies, beginning in 1961. This project will include
