Supply-Citizenship and Immigration a re-survey of reserves in northern Ontario carried out by the forestry branch during the period 1949 to 1952.
It is also planned to continue the forest inventory of reserves in British Columbia this coming season. This project, under the supervision of a firm of forest consultants, has so far produced survey reports covering approximately one half the forested acreage. During this past winter a forest survey on the Restigouche Indian reserve in Quebec was also carried out by a forest consultant firm.
The services of the forestry branch of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources and provincial forestry departments are utilized to a wide extent. The over-all policy is to bring under forest management as much of the timbered area of Indian reserves as possible with a view, where possible, to placing reserve forestry on a perpetual yield basis.
The Indian Act provides for the transfer to bands of control over revenue fund expenditures. Some progress has been made in this direction. Three bands in the southern Ontario region have taken over such control, and one band in British Columbia has agreed to assume similar responsibility. Others are giving serious consideration to the matter. The taking over of responsibility for management and control of revenue fund expenditures has been proposed to several additional band councils, but it will be appreciated that this is a matter that cannot be pressed unduly. The desire for greater responsibility and control over their own affairs must in the final analysis emanate from the Indian community itself.
Meanwhile, improved administrative services for Indians residing in more remote areas is occupying the attention of my department. For example, at the start of this fiscal year a new administrative region was established to service Indians in the Northwest Territories. This is to be known as the district of Mackenzie region with headquarters at Fort Smith. This step has been taken to provide better supervision over the affairs of the Indian population in the Northwest Territories. Under the district of Mackenzie region an additional agency will come into operation at Fort Simpson. ;

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to make any extended general references in reply to the statement that the hon. lady has just made. I recognize that in view of the fact there is a joint committee of the two houses sitting discussing the Indian Act and Indian matters generally there is perhaps not the same need here in this committee at this particular session for

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration extended observations which might be repetitious. Since the government has insisted on so many committees sitting at once during the session I have found it impossible to attend the Indian affairs committee without staying away from another committee where I have a more urgent responsibility. I would not like to inflict upon other hon. members a repetition of matters that may have been rather thoroughly discussed there.
I must say, as I have said on previous occasions when the minister's estimates were before the committee, that I find it much easier to agree with the minister's general approach to the Indian affairs branch of the department than I do to agree with her general approach to the problems of immigration. The minister, it seems to me, is following precisely along the lines that were established by my predecessor and hers, Mr. Harris, who really with the new Indian Act and with the new administration which accompanied it did make a very great advance in this field over what had been done before.
We all know it was one of those regrettable incidents of the second world war that the Indian affairs branch, and some other branches of the civil government did get somewhat neglected-and I do not think anybody was really to blame for this except the urgency of meeting the demands for manpower that did seem to most of us, rightly or wrongly, to be the more urgent task at that time.
However, I do want to reiterate in the most emphatic language I can the view which I hold and which I think, judging from an earlier debate in this session-you do not need to worry, Mr. Chairman; I am not going to seek to traverse that subject-seemed to be the general view of the house, namely the idea that the goal of our policy should be voluntary integration of Indians just as rapidly as that can be accomplished. I do not think there should be any compulsion whatever put upon them. I think that has to be made abundantly clear because, rightly or wrongly-I am afraid sometimes rightly-a lot of Indians have the feeling that what we mean by integration is neglect, and this is certainly not what I mean. What I mean by integration is that I should like to see the Canadian citizenship of Indians become so much a matter of pride that that would be what they would be most proud of, without, of course, neglecting in any way that appropriate pride of ancestry, that proper pride in their individual characteristics and in their traditions, many of which traditions we would not, I think, find it unprofitable to follow.
Integration is not possible without encouraging in the Indians a sense of selfreliance. It seems to me that in order to get

that sense of self-reliance that is going to be essential if the Indians are to feel they do not have to regard their reserves and certain other special privileges as a kind of crutch in life, it must be based on a feeling of genuine equality. This means that they must have available to them equal opportunities and if we are going to be fair to them at all I would say a little better than equal opportunities for education. It also means that they must have more than just education. They must have an increased capacity and an increased desire instilled in them to manage their own affairs and also to share in managing the affairs of the community in which they live. Therefore, I am very glad indeed to hear the minister say that this business-one could wish it were something else but it is one of those inescapable necessities at the present time-of giving to the Indians a greater responsibility for the distribution of relief, paying relief in cash instead of in kind, is one step in the right direction.
Any kind of step that can be taken to give band councils more responsibility and more capacity to look after their own affairs and to establish a less paternalistic approach to the whole matter is, in my view, highly desirable. The other thing we have to recognize increasingly is that because of modern sanitation, because of better housing for which we are all very grateful, the relatively high birth rate among the Indian population in Canada is resulting in a rapid increase in the Indian population, which means that every year there must be available to the Indians substantially more jobs, or more economic opportunities of one kind and another than there were in the previous year if they are simply to maintain their existing standard of living and not even to increase it. We cannot be satisfied if they alone maintain their existing standard of living. Certainly most of these economic opportunities and most of these jobs are not going to be found on the reserves. This is why it seems to me that next to education the most important thing in the Indian affairs department is the conscious development of economic opportunities, the encouragement of the Indians to accept employment and the encouragement of employers to accept Indians, which is just as important.
I want to say again, as I think I have said every year, that during the time I was minister I had the benefit, which I am told the minister has not got for many reasons, of the services in this field of Mr. Mel Jack who in my view had the right conception of this matter and the right attitude to it, the attitude that we must not be too paternalistic, that we must encourage the Indians to

plunge in and take these jobs and must encourage employers to make these opportunities available and treat the Indians like their other employees, show them consideration but also expect them to pull their weight. All these things which were started at that time have proved to be a surprising success.
I remember the difficulties we had at first in getting farmers in Alberta to consider having the Indians help them with their sugar beets. I understand that the farmers now almost come on hands and knees to the minister. I remember the first discussions I had with some representatives of the mining community in northern Ontario who wanted me to facilitate a search for miners in Europe. I asked them why they should go to Europe when right on their own doorstep they had these original Canadians who needed jobs. They thought I was being very ridiculous.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Did you say that?

I said that and I was supported by Mr. Mel Jack who followed up the matter. As a matter of fact, we did persuade some of these people to accept Indians and they were astonished at their success. Of course, some of the Indians did not succeed but some immigrants do not succeed and some other native-born Canadians do not succeed. There is nothing unique about a failure, but in one or two of these cases there was in the beginning something that was close to being unique about success.
I believe that these two things, education and normal employment in the integrated Canadian society, are the road and the only road to the creation of a healthy, respectable and prideful relationship between the Indians and the other citizens of Canada. I am afraid it will not be true no matter what efforts are made but nevertheless I hope that some of the younger members of the house will live long enough to see the day when the minister's office of superintendent general of Indian affairs is no longer needed, when we will no longer need an Indian affairs branch and when no distinction of any kind will be made between Indians and other Canadians.

Mr. Chairman, in rising to make a few remarks on this item may I say that I hope the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was not including himself among those who might not live long enough to see the discontinuance of the office of superintendent general of Indian affairs. I should like to see that happy event occur with the greatest possible speed, not that I want to see the present minister, as long as she remains minister, partially unemployed but
16, 1960
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration because I think that this is the most advantageous result to which we can look forward. The one branch of the government with which I have perhaps had more contact and more correspondence than any other is the Indian affairs branch. I sometimes wonder whether the director, Colonel Jones, does not get a bit fed up with hearing from me, and I should like to express publicly to Colonel Jones and the other officials of the Indian affairs branch in its various divisions my appreciation of their kindness, the speed with which they have answered all my queries and the consideration they have given to any problems I have brought to their attention. I am sure that any other hon. members who have had occasion to discuss matters with officials of the branch will wish to express the same appreciation.
I should also like to express my appreciation to the minister for having established a new agency at Terrace which is located in the community from which I come. This will be of great assistance in the departmental administration of the affairs of the Indian bands now in the Terrace agency and which before were some considerable distance from the agency under which they were placed. I am sure the new agency will assist immeasurably in dealing with the problems of the Indian people in the bands concerned. In addition, other Indian agencies will have less administrative work to do with respect to these bands.
The minister referred to the institution of the practice of making welfare payments by cash or cheque rather than in kind. She indicated that this had been instituted in some agencies and that during the coming year the intention is to expand the making of welfare payments by cheque. I have had some communication with the department about this matter and I should like to see the practice extended as soon as possible, especially with respect to the Babine agency whose headquarters are at Hazelton, also in my constituency. It may be that steps are already underway to institute the making of welfare payments by cheque in this agency.
The reason I should like to see it done there as soon as possible is that the Indian people who come under the Babine agency are in close touch with and speak the same language as many of those coming under the Skeena river agency and the Terrace agency. They follow the same line of work, fishing, and at this time of the year or a little earlier they congregate in Prince Rupert and other coastal points. I understand that the system of payment by cheque is in effect in both the Terrace and Skeena river agencies and this causes some conflict because the Indian

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration people of the Babine agency meet their relatives and friends, find that they are receiving welfare payments by cheque and want to know why this is not so in the Babine agency.
I would appreciate it if this could be speeded up as much as possible.
The minister and the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate also made reference to educational facilities and opportunities for our Indian people. To me this is also a most important aspect of the work of the Indian affairs branch. I am pleased to se the continuing increase in the amount of the appropriation for educational purposes and opportunities. In the past not only the Indians but other people have been denied the opportunity to obtain an education or have been restricted to a certain degree of education. To my mind this is an important factor in the advancement of our native Indians and in assisting them to become integrated and to advance to the position where they will be in the same class and on the same footing as those who are not Indians.
' The minister made some reference to surveying reserves for timber purposes and this is a commendable approach. With respect to the sale of reserve lands, I should like to emphasize that everything possible should be done, having regard to the circumstances, to see that generally the policy of the department is to discourage the sale of Indian reserve land as much as possible and to concentrate, if possible, on leases or rental arrangements. We have seen an instance or two in which the sale of reserve lands or part of the reserve lands has not been of any long term economic or other advantage to the Indians themselves. I think, perhaps, if the policy were one of not encouraging the sale of reserve lands it would be most beneficial in the long run to the Indian people themselves and to society as a whole.
In so far as the Indian affairs committee is concerned I, like the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, sit on two other committees, the meetings of which coincide in point of time with the meetings of the Indian affairs committee. I have found it difficult at times to be in boths places at once and, therefore, have had to miss some of the proceedings of the Indian affairs committee, which is regrettable. However, I believe all members of the committee who have attended the meetings have been impressed by the calibre of the Indians who have appeared before that committee, by the clarity with which they have expressed themselves, the manner in which their briefs were prepared and presented, and the understanding that they have had of the points and problems which they have presented. As I have said, this


impressed me greatly, as I am sure it impressed other members of the committee.
One of the things which I believe we must attempt to develop, and this has been emphasized on a number of occasions by a number of people-this is not an original thought of mine-is the need to develop in Canada the highest possible degree of mutual understanding and respect. Probably the emphasis should be placed on that phase of mutual understanding and respect that is necessary on the part of non-Indian people generally, because there are many non-Indian people in Canada who because of geographic factors or economic factors do not come into contact with the Indian people. Consequently they have a very scanty understanding, if any, of the way of life of Indian people or their problems. The more that we can bring the non-Indian people to understand, respect and appreciate the cultural background, history and heritage of our Indian people, the better opportunity there will be in the future for the Indian people to play a greater role in our society as well as contributing to their own welfare and their own well-being.
Perhaps as a part of this program we should participate as much as possible in teaching the Indian children themselves as much as we know of the history of their own people so that they, too, can understand and appreciate their own cultural heritage, their own cultural background. I know from talking to Indian people living in villages which are relatively isolated that their knowledge of their background, their history, was greater than that of Indian people who have been in close contact with society or with non-Indians because they have been close to urban areas and their contact with their own people has been less than in the other case. There is a tendency for these children to forget or to lack any understanding of their own people and their own background. Perhaps this could also be a contributing factor to the development of that mutual respect and understanding of each other that is so necessary, and in conjunction with the educational approach perhaps could result in progress for our Indian people toward self-sufficiency and toward regarding themselves less as an inferior race and more as a proud race.
There has been some reference to the question of enfranchisement, which is another factor connected with this whole problem. I certainly congratulate the minister on her approach to this question. I believe that we should, without hesitation and without any qualms, eliminate the compulsory section of the Indian Act which deals with enfranchisement. I refer to the section of the act under

which an Indian or a band can be enfranchised compulsorily whether or not they want it. I think this section should be removed from the act. I do not believe there is much purpose in retaining the other enfranchisement section. This is a recent thought that I have developed after listening to the presentations made to the committee and as a result of discussions I have had outside the committee. I know that there will be problems arising from the complete elimination of any reference in the act to enfranchisement. This does not necessarily have the connotation which we normally attach to the word "enfranchisement", which means the Indian is no longer an Indian within the meaning of the act; is no longer a member of the band; has no longer a right on the reserve and is in the same class as non-Indian people.
I believe that Indians should have complete freedom to live upon the reserve or to leave that reserve, to come and go as they please, a freedom which they have at the moment and which many Indians exercise. I know a number of them, and some of them are in very responsible positions in society. Some of them are still members of the band, although they have not been on the reserve for many years. They still retain that connection, and some of them live many hundreds of miles from their home reserve. This situation can exist at the moment.
The enfranchisement section, as I understand it, was designed to be an attraction to Indians to leave the reserve and become non-Indians, in effect, in so far as the legal definition under the Indian Act is concerned. Some of the Indians have taken advantage of this section, have become enfranchised for a variety of reasons, but these reasons I feel are gradually diminishing. The more we progress toward the removal of the restrictive sections of the Indian Act, the more we move toward equality of status, the less reason there is for the enfranchisement section. I know there will be complications here in so far as band funds are concerned, and whether the Indian will have the opportunity of taking with him his per capita share from those band funds. However, I do not believe the difficulty is insurmountable. There are various ways of overcoming it.
I think this is the understanding of the Indians that we want to have, and an appreciation of the fact they have a vested interest in this country, more so than I have or other non-Indians have. We should recognize this fact and say to the Indian that he can continue to live on the reserve if he so desires or he can leave it, but it is not necessary for him to give up entirely his
16, 1960
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration Indian status and thus cut himself off completely from ever returning to the reserve or to his Indian status. If you remove the enfranchisement sections from the act, as I say, this problem can be overcome.
So far as local control is concerned this too will be a contributing factor in the integration process. I draw attention especially to the word "integration" because it has been given the connotation that the Indian must become one of us and forget all about the fact that he is an Indian. I do not mean that by the word integration. I mean that in order to add to the respect of the Indian himself and in order to add to the mutual respect and understanding which we should have for each other, and in order that he may overcome what inferiority complex may have been developed in him through the activities of non-Indians, we should to a very large measure as quickly as possible and as much as possible give to the Indian and the band councils the right to run their own affairs. I think the minister said that there were three bands in southern Ontario and one in British Columbia, but in any event there were four bands in Canada who now have control over their own band funds without any authority from the minister to administer them. This is working in the direction of local control and of self-sufficiency, self-development and self-operation of their own affairs. I think this should be expanded as quickly as possible.
I know that errors will be made, and that is understandable. There is not a municipal council in existence in Canada that has not made an error at some time or other about the disposition of its revenue. I do not think there has ever been a government of Canada that in some way or another has not made some error in the administration of moneys which it collects or spends, or any provincial government either, for that matter. I know that I have made a number of mistakes in the manner in which I spend my money, and I do not seem to learn from them either. But the more we give the bands the administration of their own affairs and the making of their own bylaws on the reserve and the right to expend their own moneys, the more we will be asking them to learn and the quicker will they be able to develop those abilities to reach a higher status in society.
I should like to make one other reference to those sections of the Indian Act which deal with the liquor question. I believe it was at the last session when another hon. gentleman held the position you now hold Mr. Chairman, that I got into some difficulties when making reference to some individuals in society who had provided liquor for some Indians, but I do not intend to get into that
5034	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration field today although it is still a valid point. The provisions in the Indian Act relating to liquor for Indians are such that the initiative rests with the provincial governments and it is initially up to the provincial governments to decide on the liquor question with regard to Indians and decide to what extent Indians may be in posession of liquor within the province.
Perhaps I can relate this briefly. The first of these approaches is for the provincial government by proclamation to declare that an Indian can consume liquor in licensed premises only. That is the only place he can have a drink. He cannot buy liquor in a liquor store or a wine store, or whatever it is, in a particular province and take it home. He cannot come into my house and have a drink with me because that would be illegal; it is within the province.
The second step, which is again by proclamation, is that the Indian can be in possession of liquor within the province but not on the reserve. This would allow an Indian to be able to consume liquor in a licensed premises such as a beer parlour or cocktail bar and would also give him the right to come into my home at my invitation and have a drink with me. It would also give him the right to buy liquor at a liquor store and transport it to his place of residence if it was not on a reserve, but he could not take it on the reserve.
The final and complete authority is that he be allowed to have liquor on the reserve if the majority of the band members vote by plebiscite or referendum to have it on that particular reserve.
In various parts of Canada there are dif-ferents degrees of availability to Indians of liquor, and I would like to deal with one which exists in British Columbia because I think it is rather an asinine one. It has operated there ever since 1951 or 1952 when the provincial government proclaimed that the Indian had the right to consume liquor in licensed premises, and that is as far as he could go. He cannot have it on the reserve or have it in his possession anywhere in the province; he can only go into a beer parlour or into a cocktail bar, buy a drink and drink it there. This has been the law for a number of years.
However, the attorney general of British Columbia, Attorney General Bonner, has said it is entirely up to the Indians whether they want liquor or not, that it has nothing to do with his government. I submit that Attorney General Bonner is just passing the buck and refusing to deal with the question, or he does not know what he is talking about


and has not paid any attention to the Indian Act or the liquor act of British Columbia. It is at this stage entirely within the jurisdiction of the Indian act of British Columbia to proclaim the next step of his being in possession within the province.
Would the hon. membei permit a question?
Yes.
Did he ever attempt to discuss this matter with the premier of British Columbia?

I have tried on a number of occasions to discuss many matters with the premier of British Columbia and I have had the same degree of success as did the Minister of Finance. It just is not possible to discuss anything with Premier Bennett.
I thought that would be the answer.
In fact I have written him letters about a number of things, I have still not had a reply, and the last letters were written four or five years ago.
They must have got lost.

That is not the Post Office Department's fault either because I know he did get the letters.
So that this is merely a buck passing game that Attorney General Bonner is engaged in in the province of British Columbia, or it indicates how inefficient he is. He should not be in that position if he does not know about the liquor act of British Columbia or about the Indian Act.
There is another even more ridiculous system which exists in British Columbia with respect to liquor and perhaps this system also exists in other provinces, but I do not know. Right now by proclamation of the province an Indian can consume liquor in a licensed premises. The Indian Act calls it "a public place". However, if an Indian who is a veteran belongs to the Canadian Legion which has a liquor licence, while he is allowed to consume liquor in a beer parlour he cannot go into the licensed premises of the Canadian Legion. That shows you how ridiculous these things are.
I raised this matter with Colonel McGugan, chairman of the liquor control board of British Columbia and with the minister, and I had correspondence with them and with the Canadian Legion about it, but it remains a fact. This again is an overstrict and perhaps foolish interpretation given by the provincial government authorities. Let hon. members imagine, if they can, an Indian

who is a veteran having the right to go into a public place to consume liquor and yet not having the right to go into his own Canadian Legion to which he belongs and which, perhaps, he helped to build and to finance. We can see how foolish is the application of our liquor laws to our Indian native people.
As far as these liquor laws are concerned, I think Indians should have the same rights, privileges and responsibilities as everybody else. I can never forget the conclusive argument used by Mr. Frank Calder, C.C.F. M.L.A. in British Columbia when dealing with people who do not want Indians to have liquor. Frank used to say: yes, it is true. The Indian, when he becomes drunk, becomes obnoxious; he wobbles all over the place; he cannot control his emotions, uses unkind language, wants to fight; in fact, he is almost as bad as a drunken white man. This, I think, sums it up. There is not too much difference between one and the other.
If we could arrange that Indians should have the same rights and the same responsibilities with regard to liquor as do other citizens of Canada we would be taking another step on the road to equality and eventually we might come to the point mentioned by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate when we would no longer have to address the hon. lady in her capacity as superintendent general of Indian affairs.

I should like to draw to the attention of the minister a problem which I brought up in 1958 when the present Minister of Justice was acting minister of citizenship and immigration. This has to do with the administration of justice on the Six Nations reserve which is adjacent to the city of Brantford which I represent.
Before anyone becomes excited about this item of justice being dealt with by the federal government, I want to emphasize the fact that the Territorial Lands Act made the Six Nations reserve a part of the county of Brant for everything but municipal purposes. That is the reason we get no taxes whatsoever from the township of Tuscarora to help toward the cost of the administration of justice in the county of Brant. Both the city of Brantford and the county of Brant have to pay the full cost of maintaining magistrates courts, county courts and supreme court hearings if cases come up on the reserve.
I made quite a statement in 1958, and after that was given some publicity in the newspapers and brought to the attention of the provincial government they did come through with a grant of $1 per capita up to $3,500 to help toward these costs. One of the problems I brought out at that time was the fact
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration that in the period I was talking about there was $3,390 paid in fees in the magistrate's court. Of this, $2,200 went to the dominion government and $689 went back to the Six Nations reserve on account of the classification of cases that came before the court. It seems a point of irony that the federal government, which does not contribute one cent toward these costs, should get the biggest share of the fines taken in this magistrate's court. I have just a short statement of some of the costs and how it works out. In the county and the city for this last year it worked out at $1.79 per capita. That is the net direct charge for the administration of justice, shared by the county and the city in 1959.
Also we have quite a problem in trying to find out how many people there actually are on the reserve. If you talk to some officials they say there are perhaps 3,500, but other officials, who like to feel they have a somewhat bigger job than some people appreciate, claim there are 6,000. This makes quite a difference in the grants we get from the Ontario government and it makes a big difference to the cost of administering justice in the county and magistrate's courts.
The city and the county are both responsible for the maintenance of juveniles committed to training schools from their respective municipalities, and included in the administration of justice figure above is a charge for one boy and one girl who are not band Indians. The cost was charged to the county of Brant and shared by the city and the county-it amounted to $501.30. There are also the juvenile and family courts. The net direct charge for these and for the probation office in 1959 was $5,469, shared by the city and the county. The people of Tuscarora and the Six Nations reserve use this court and it is available to them just as it is to the people of the city and the county. In addition, the court house supplies heating, maintenance and other features which are necessary for the sittings of these juvenile and family courts.
There is another problem. You will remember that last year when we had the uprising down on the reserve-quite a turnout that was down there-a number of young chaps were arrested and brought into court. But through the intervention of some individuals the cases were dismissed. However, the costs of the crown attorney who prosecuted in these cases have not been picked up for payment by anybody and therefore they went back to the city and county for payment. I do not think it should be the responsibility of the city or the county to pay costs when cases are dismissed.
We have also to pay for the supreme court sittings with regard to any criminal cases
5036	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration that come from the reserve. Last year a resident of the reserve was arrested for murder and lodged in the county jail. She was not in her right mind. That meant we had to have matrons on 24-hour duty at all times. We also had, finally, to take her to St. Thomas where she had to be examined by doctors, and the extra cost over and above the direct charges such as maintenance while in jail, constables' attendance in court, the crown attorney's fees, sheriff's fees and sheriff's office expenses amounted to $3,113.
There is money available in the Six Nations fund. They assume they are wards of the federal government, and the federal government showed that they realized that this is part of their jurisdiction because not too long ago-some few years ago-they put the R.C.M.P. down there to police this reserve. So I think it is only fair and just that the federal government should make money available for the Six Nations Indians or the township of Tuscarora to pay their share of magistrate's court and county court costs to the city and to the county of Brant. This has been a problem we have had to put up with for a long number of years. I should like the minister to take note of the fact that we would like to have a fair share of the cost come from this reserve.
Another problem I should like to bring to the attention of the minister is that of fire protection on the reserve. Indeed there is no fire protection on the reserve at this time. Some day we are going to be faced with a serious fire on this reserve that will result in the death of children and grown-ups and because of the lack of fire protection there the cry will go out that the fire departments of the township of Brantford and Brantford city should have gone to the reserve and looked after the fire. The fire department of the city of Brantford has responded to calls on the reserve but it was not able to obtain an agreement with the council there to pay for these calls and so the service has been discontinued.
After the township established its volunteer fire brigade it responded to the first call on the reserve and was told it would be paid for it. Unfortunately the promise was not kept and the township has never been paid. Just recently another fire broke out on the reserve and a call for urgent assistance went out to the township fire department. The assurance was given that the township would be paid for the call. After the call was completed and the fire put out the township was informed by the reserve that there was no money available to pay for fire protection. The cost of the call amounted to over $300 in wages for the men


and equipment. The township has now absolutely cut off the reserve from any more calls and thus the reserve is left without any fire protection whatever.
I feel it would be the better part of wisdom to have some kind of fire truck-a pumper, perhaps, even a used one obtained through war assets or something like that- put on the reserve to give the people there some protection. I know that the men on the reserve would be only too willing to man the engine. It would also give them a sense of pride in ownership in having a fire truck down there to look after their own fires.
I have been on the reserve several times. One bad feature of sending a fire truck to the reserve from the township of Brantford is that the bridge on the main road leading into reserve bears a sign indicating that the maximum load is eight tons. When a call comes through from the reserve we are asked to send down a fire truck costing $25,000, carrying several hundred gallons of water and weighing considerably over eight tons. If the bridge should collapse and the truck be destroyed the township would have to replace it because it seems impossible to obtain money from federal funds or through any other means for fire protection on the reserve.
I wish to speak now on behalf of the people on the reserve. They are in great need of a bridge across the Grand river at Onondaga. To get from the reserve to the eastern part of the city of Brantford or any point east of the city necessitates travelling through the downtown area of the city in order to get back to a point just across the river. A small part of the reserve is located across the river in the township of Onondaga. To travel from one part of the reserve to the other part across the river involves travelling several miles. I know the Indians have a certain amount of money for use in the construction and maintenance of roads and that sort of thing. The Ontario government contributes to the same extent it does to other municipalities in the province. They do not, however, have sufficient money in their annual road budget to provide a bridge over the river. I urge the minister and her officials to investigate the problem and to help the people on the reserve in this respect. I know anything that could be done would be greatly appreciated.
Before taking my seat I wish to emphasize again the first problem I raised. We would appreciate assistance from the federal government to meet the cost of the administration of justice in the city of Brantford.

Mr. Chairman, if no other hon. member of the committee wants to

speak in more general terms I should like to say something about a specific matter concerning which the minister will not be surprised to hear me make some observations. There has recently been a great deal of publicity in the press about the activities of a certain corporation which is called Dimensional Investments Limited which, according to the information I have, bought for the sum of $6,521,946 a considerable part of the Sarnia Indian reserve.
The first thing I want to say about this matter is that for a somewhat smaller part of this reserve-there was not very much difference in the area and it was somewhat similar if my information is correct and, if it is not, the minister will correct me because she will have the facts-I had virtually completed a sale which was approved by the band in 1957 for the sum of $7,902,000. The sale fell through because the purchasers were not in the final analysis able to put up the money.
I may say that I was very relieved when that sale fell through because in the period during which it was being negotiated I had very considerable doubts about whether it was a wise thing to sell this property at all. I discussed this on more than one occasion with the officials. I said, here is this very valuable property on the edge of one of the fastest growing industrial communities in Canada, a community which is growing very largely because of expenditures made by the federal government during the war and which gives every appearance of continuing to grow very rapidly far into the future because of the very modern industries located there, industries such as synthetics industries, petrochemical industries, ordinary chemical industries for that matter, and others. I could not get it out of my head all through this period that we should not sell this land at all, that it was too valuable to be sold and that it should remain indefinitely a trust for the Indian band who occupied it.
I made up my mind when the sale fell through that if I had any further responsibility in the matter-I was relieved of that responsibility not long after-I would not again consent to any of these sales regardless of the price, that the proper way to deal with these matters was to create a trust and enter into long term leases so that the Indians could maintain a continuing interest in what was originally theirs.
It is true that according to land values at that time the sum of nearly $8 million we were proposing to sell this for was a very good price indeed. If the Indian reserve had been ordinary property on which taxes had to be paid no doubt I would have agreed
16, 1960	5037
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration that it was a very sound business transaction. I am not questioning that at all. In retrospect I still think it was. But when we consider that Indian reserves are not liable to taxation and that it costs nothing to hold the property except any loss of revenue that there may be-the normal business considerations do not enter into these transactions in that particular respect; that is to say there is not the same overhead that has to be met in continuing to hold the land-I must say I am surprised that the present government should have been willing to agree to the sale of this land for approximately $1,400,000 less than the previous administration thought was a fair price for it.
I would question the transaction on that ground alone if there were no other circumstances connected with it; but the circumstances connected with this transaction, of which we do not know all yet, are such that one has even graver doubts, in the light of some of the other information that has been published and is uncontradicted. According to the best information I can get, the average price per acre paid for this land- the whole of this land that was sold to Dimensional from this reserve-was $2,093. This land was not all sold at exactly the same price per acre, and part of this land was resold to the Ontario Hydro almost before the ink was dry on the first contract for a price that works out to $6,944 an acre.
With respect to the part of the land that was taken by Hydro, the price received from Dimensional by the Indians was $2,000, so that by executing one contract and then reselling to an agency of the crown in Ontario this company made a profit of practically $5,000 an acre, which the Indians ought to have had if the land was worth that much. If that land was worth that much to the Hydro, a provident administration of the Indian affairs department would have got that much for it and they would not have sold it for less.
I am not saying it was worth that to Hydro at all; I am not saying that, because it is a matter that is not under the jurisdiction of this parliament and it is being discussed in another place before a royal commission, and I do not propose to argue for one minute about that. The Ontario Hydro may have paid three and a half times too much for this land, and the only defence the minister will have is to say that, because she sold it for $2,000 and promptly the Ontario Hydro paid $5,000 an acre more for it. That is two and a half times as much. So that either the minister sold it at a bargain or Ontario Hydro paid an extravagant price. We cannot get away from that.

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
The minister cannot plead, of course, that she did not know the Ontario Hydro wanted this land, or at least that her officials did not know that the Ontario Hydro wanted the land, because that is on the record. It is on the record that certain approaches were made by Ontario Hydro. The minister has made it very clear, if I remember correctly-and I am speaking here from memory, and if I am wrong the minister will correct me at once and I will make the correction-that the Ontario Hydro never came to her or to the department to have this land expropriated.
That is right.

It also has been published that they did approach the government, the Indian affairs branch at any rate, with a view to discussing the possibilities of its being acquired by negotiation. At least, that is what I have been informed and if I am wrong about that I think it ought to be denied right away.

Mr. Chairman, there is some element of truth in that but what I should like to point out is that it was not a decision of the department, it was a decision of the Indians themselves. They refused to sell this parcel of land to Hydro because it cut right through the centre of the block of land of which they wished to dispose. It took the very best part right from the centre; it depreciated the value of the other property around it, and they said no, they wanted to sell the whole block and, as my hon. friend knows, there is some land in that particular block that is not worth very much.

Some of the land may not be worth very much for growing cherries. This land is in an area where all the land is worth a great deal because it is in a growing industrial area and it does not really matter much in a growing industrial area unless there is an Alp, and there are no Alps around Sarnia. It does not matter much whether it is good land or swamp land. With modern machinery you can soon fix that up; therefore, I am not very much impressed by that particular argument.

As the act stands at the present time the minister, being a minister of the crown, in my opinion is the one person who should be administering Indian lands in trust for Indians, because land is held by the crown in trust for them. This also applied to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate when he was in the position the hon. lady is in at the moment.
Holding lands in trust indicates that that trust should be carefully looked after and the interests of the Indians protected in each instance. I am not going to get into a discussion with respect to the sale of this particular piece of land at Sarnia. However, I have had occasion to come across sales of land on Indian reserves in the past which would lead me to believe that perhaps the interests of the Indians have not been fully and properly protected, and perhaps in the initial instance this falls on the shoulders of the Indian protector or agent in explaining to band councils and to bands the effects which might accrue from the sale of any particular parcel of band land or land of a locatee.
I have had occasion to become interested in at least three particular sales which come to mind offhand over which difficulties have arisen after the sale had taken place, and this would indicate that the interests of the Indian had not been fully protected before the sale. If this continues it is leaving the impression with the Indian that perhaps

he should not even consider selling any additional parcels of land because he would end up on the short side of things when the sale is over.
As an example, one individual, a locatee on the Hazelton reserve, about ten years ago or so sold some land or agreed to sell land of his to the local school board for the purpose of building a school. As I understand it, the money was paid promptly by the school board to the Indian affairs branch and it took this individual, Mr. Ben Mackenzie, some seven years from the time the land was sold to the school board and the school board paid the money to the Indian affairs branch until he received payment. Todd and Sons than he did for the Indians because it was not until subsequent to the sale and closing down of the cannery that the Indians realized the full impact of the sale of this land. As I said in my opening remarks, I think it should be the policy of the department to attempt to promote leases and rentals, if that is desirable, rather than sales because a sale is such a final transaction. I endorse that view completely and I have always been of that opinion. I am only sorry that they did not have the same interest during the time that my friend and his colleagues were in office. Perhaps we will profit now by the experience gained in such cases as that on the Kitasoo Indian reserve to which I have referred.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few brief remarks with regard to one or two problems facing the Indians of our country that have been brought to my attention. Some of these problems I have observed myself and others have been brought to my attention by people living in northern Manitoba. At the outset I should like to express my appreciation to the minister, the director of the branch, Colonel Jones, and the Indian agents in northern Manitoba and their field men for the co-operation they have given me during the past three years. I should also like to tell the minister that the people of this area were very pleased that she was able to visit northern Manitoba last summer. She was not able to go to all the reserves and we hope that she will be able to come back to that area in the near future.
Personally I do not believe that the people of Canada generally realize what a tremendous amount of work is being carried out by the Indian affairs branch in an endeavour to solve the many problems with which the Indians are faced. One only has to make a few trips into these outlying areas with an Indian agent and meet the band leaders and councillors to come to a realization of just how much work the branch is doing to solve the many problems and, believe me, there are still many to be solved.
There is one specific problem very evident in the northern part of the country to which I should like to see serious consideration given. I may say that I brought a specific case to the attention of the director of the branch very recently. We were not able to do too much about it because possibly the matter was left too late but we will be forever faced with the same problem unless something is done. The problem has to do with the situation that arises when the Indian affairs branch and other departments such as northern affairs and national defence are planning the construction of establishments in outlying areas of northern Canada. I refer to the construction of hospitals, nursing stations, Indian residential schools and so on. In their construction one thing that must be provided is an adequate electric power supply. In many cases when such buildings are constructed they are located close to an Indian reservation or possibly a small settlement inhabited by people of the Indian race.

When planning the power requirements for these establishments I should like to see consideration given to making a preliminary survey of the possibility of providing for the electric power requirements of the Indian people who live adjacent to the hospital, school or whatever the building is. I realize that when plans for power installations are planned an effort is made to arrive at a reasonable estimate of how much power may be needed by the particular building in the future and allowance is made for that but I cannot see why it would not be possible to make allowance for additional power for the Indian people living adjacent these areas. If provision is not made for such power when planning these government establishments the people in these areas will be a long time before they get the benefit of electric power.
The reason I bring this matter to the attention of the minister at this time is that it is my understanding that up until this time it has been the feeling of the department, possibly a reasonable one, that to do what I have suggested would create a tremendous amount of extra work for them which is not actually in their field. It is claimed that it would create work in making surveys of the necessary extensions of power, that it would create an obligation on the department to establish the rates to be charged and would also create obligations with respect to the distribution of the power and collection of accounts.
That does seem like quite a large assignment to give any government department but I think there is a good solution for that, especially in Manitoba, and I do not see why the same solution could not be applied in other provinces confronted with the same problem. I have very good assurance from the Manitoba power commission that they would welcome the opportunity of purchasing excess power from any source if there was a reasonable market for that power in the vicinity. They have told me they would be quite willing not only to purchase the power but to arrange for its distribution and to set the rates and collect the accounts. With such an arrangement having been suggested by the Manitoba power commission, I think that many of the problems are overcome.
I should like to say once again that generally government departments do not take some of these things into consideration and do not realize that they have an obligation, as government departments, to the people of Canada living in these outlying areas to bring to them some of these amenities of life. If we do not do that, we are not doing our job. I know that this is a problem which exists all over the northern part of our country. I believe it is only reasonable to assume that most 79951-0-319J

I have just one brief remark to make, Mr. Chairman. There has been some reference on several occasions during the debate this evening to people misleading the house. I think there was one thing the hon. member for Trinity kept saying repeatedly and that was that this company which purchased this land from the Indians in Sarnia had a capitalization of $40,000. The inference that anyone who is not conversant with the technicalities of corporation law would draw is that the only assets of the company were $40,000. This is most certainly not the case.
It is customary, in the province of Ontario when a company is incorporated to incorporate with a capitalization of $40,000. It simply means that the par value of the authorized shares to be issued then or at some time in the future is $40,000. It has no relationship whatever to the actual assets of the company. I am sure the hon. member must know that.

On the contrary, I was attempting to lead the committee. The matter of capitalization, as the hon. member for Oxford has just said, is not necessarily indicative of the total assets or net worth of the company. This was a newly incorporated company, however, which had no other assets. The total of its assets was limited by the extent of its capitalization, under the law of the province of Ontario, so that its assets were equal to its total capitalization or something less than that. No financial documents whatever were filed by the company, as has been ably demonstrated, to indicate it had any assets whatever, even within the $40,000 of its capitalization or over and beyond that. I am surprised that a learned counsel would not be able to determine this for himself. I hope I will not have to retain him to do legal work for any company with which I am connected.

I think it is quite irresponsible for the minister to authorize the sale of millions of dollars worth of land held in trust for an Indian band to a newly formed company with a capitalization of $40,000 and with no demonstration of assets, even to that extent.

There have been a lot of very peculiar statements made here tonight, and between the pseudo real estate valuators who cannot even add and the financial experts who do


not know the difference between capitalization and assets we have had ourselves quite a field day.
I suppose the hon. lady could set the record right.
Oh, I cannot be bothered. I am here in my capacity as a minister to defend my department. I am not here to give lessons in economics and real estate valuation to hon. members.
I rise on a question of privilege.
Sit down.

The hon. lady has said that she is not here to give lessons in economics. Nobody wants lessons in economics, but we are entitled in this committee to an accounting of the business of this country, particularly when it is business done in trust for the original inhabitants of this country, and that is what the hon. lady refuses to give; indulging in innuendo and insinuations instead of dealing with facts.

All right, Mr. Chairman, I shall do my best to put the record straight. However, I cannot be held responsible for those who will not listen or will not understand. Back in the time when my hon. friend was charged with the responsibility of this department he tells us that he had an offer of $8 million for this land.
Approximately $7,902,000.
All right, we will not quibble over $100,000. He never got one plugged nickel, not one.
That is quite right.

Ultimately the people who were supposed to have given this offer withdrew, after having held up the sale of the land for a considerable time to any other prospective purchaser, or if they did not, the minister did in the hope of getting $8 million. They decided on one of two things; either that they did not have $8 million or that the land was not worth it.
In the meantime the Indians, having been encouraged by the minister to think there was a sale going on, went out and bought sundry things-automobiles, deep freezes, electric refrigerators, washing machines, all manner of things, and got themselves well and truly in debt. And the sale fell through.
Ultimately another group came along and offered to buy this property, and I think it is no secret that their first offer was considerably lower than the price at which the agreement was drawn up.
I would hope so.
The hon. member would hope it was lower?
I hope the hon. lady would get more than the first offer.

I have not been in business for more years than I like to admit without learning a few tricks from the trade.
In any event the Indians, quite properly, were concerned about their financial obligations. They had no intention of hiding behind the protection offered them in the act and failing to live up to their financial commitments. They had been led to believe that they had a proper sale coming up. This new company came along and it made an offer. We turned that offer down. We took the precaution of engaging the services of an independent evaluator who went into this situation and gave us a full report, not only on the immediate value of the land but its potential having regard to other land which had been sold in the vicinity, having regard also to other land that was available for sale in the vicinity and taking into account the projected rate of industrial progress which was anticipated. Finally we received from them an evaluation and that evaluation was $5,500,000.
We were not satisfied completely with that so we asked the officials of the Veterans Land Act if they would give us an evaluation quite independently, without any reference to the firm which had made an evaluation and with no consultation with them. As a matter of fact they did not know who the firm was that had made an evaluation. They came up with a valuation of $5,600,000. So I think, Mr. Chairman, if we got $6,500,000 for the Indians we did pretty well.
I have no intention of arguing any case for a subsequent buyer, whether they made offers, whether they wanted anything, what they were willing to pay, what they had already done, or anything. That is no concern of mine. The thing which is my concern is that I get for the Indians the best possible price I can get having regard to the value of the land and its potential, and I maintain, Mr. Chairman, that that is what I did do. Not only did I get them the best possible price but I protected them under the terms of this contract and, as I have said before today, if this contract falls through tomorrow, if perchance the company concerned defaults in its payments, the Indians will have received something in the nature of $2,500,000 and will have sold about 10 per cent of the land which was for sale.
I cannot understand what the hon. member is talking about. I would think that there

The hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi has interjected "that is so much nonsense and you know it". All I know is that he is full of nonsense if he cannot get on his feet and put up a better argument than that. I do not happen to have some of the advantages which the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi has, but I am trying to do my best to bring up a point in which I believe and to explain why I take the attitude I do. Take Lansdowne House in the north where the population is 99 per cent Indian. They are all voting one way and when Indian agents are moving around there one has to have suspicions. I am just presenting those suspicions to the minister and suggest that in view of the pattern we are getting at election times she should issue warnings to her agents and see that no one has an opportunity to exert influence of this kind.

Under the terms of the Civil Service Act any civil servant who engages in partisan activities is subject to punishment. I cannot think of an answer to the hon. gentleman's allegation unless it is that the Indians are further advanced than we thought they were. But I can assure the hon. member that as to federal employees engaging in provincial partisan activity, the staff are in my opinion too smart for that. I do not think they would do it. If the hon. member has proof to the contrary other than the odd coincidence of figures I will be glad to look into it.

The minister can call it coincidence if she cares to. Another question I want to ask the hon. lady is an explanation of the situation at McDiarmid reserve and what the plans are there and what future efforts are going to be made if any to get the Indians at the north end of lake Nipigon and that country that feeds into there into an advantageous a situation as the Indians at McDiarmid are going to be in. We are pleased with this particular method. The Indians themselves are very satisfied, but they are concerned about their friends, relatives and other Indians at the other end of the lake and toward the Hudson Bay watershed where many of them are attracted by that kind of development just as they were from the other side of the lake.
I wondered whether there was any plan to move these people into the same kind of improved conditions. I have had letters from people in the region north of the lake-tourist agents and people like that-saying that the condition of the Indians especially in midwinter and early spring is much more serious than it has been in the lower part of the lake.
I read with interest as I am sure many hon. members did an announcement in yesterday's paper to the effect that Bishop O'Grady plans to open a new school. Despite the fact it will be partially supported by Roman Catholic church funds it will be a non-denominational school. I am interested in the long range implications of this announcement. This seems to be a break with tradition. We would appreciate an explanation of this from the minister. Does this herald a larger move of this nature in the educational field?

With regard to the McDiarmid situation and in fact the whole situation in northern Ontario my department is presently in negotiation with the province of Ontario with regard to lands and locations and so on. I can assure my hon. friend that we are most anxious that these people shall have proper facilities not only for their own comfort but for the education of their children. We cannot move any faster than our co-operative efforts with the province will dictate. However, we are not lagging at all and are proceeding as rapidly as we can.
With regard to Bishop O'Grady I find it difficult to express myself because the bishop is doing such a magnificent job. As a matter of fact he puts such pressure on the department at times that we are hard put to it to answer his demands. We know that he is working for the good of the Indians and is doing his best under difficult circumstances. In so far as co-operation with the department is concerned his situation is not different from that of anyone else. Where there is an
5054	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration effort on the part of a denominational institution to educate Indians whether in an entirely Indian school or an integrated school the department picks up the tab for the Indians' share. I must say again that I think Bishop O'Grady with his tremendous enthusiasm is doing a wonderful job for the Indians in British Columbia and I should like to have that on the record.

That seemed apparent from the story but I was interested in the fact that the school although under church support would be non-denominational. Is this the forerunner of a broader policy? Is it intended to have the non-denominational aspect of the school apply only to certain grades?

This is not our school but a church school. How it is administered is entirely up to the group concerned. I find it intriguing. I did not see the press release and can speak only from a general knowledge of the bishop's splendid work.

Mr. Chairman, like many other hon. members I have a great many Indians in my constituency although I must confess I have not had the-what shall I call it-coincidental electoral problem to which my friend the hon. member for Port Arthur referred a moment ago. However, as the minister knows an educational problem has existed for many years among the Indians in Algoma East. I am not going to speak about that at the moment because I know the department has done its best in that regard.
Perhaps before this item passes I may be permitted to express my appreciation for the courtesy and thoughtful consideration given by the officers in connection with every request I have made of them. In view of the fact that a moment ago I provoked the minister into a somewhat extreme expletive perhaps she may permit me to include her in that comment because the hon. lady has always been very courteous in dealing with the requests I have made of her.

Mr. Chairman, I believe the minister will be well aware that we have a file of correspondence going back over several years relating to the problem of Indians who are not permanently settled in Red Lake in the northern part of my area but are sort of semi-
Transients?

They are becoming
assimilated in part. This is a development which I think should be encouraged because we have mining employment and other types of employment which are more advantageous than the very uncertain type of livelihood


that is available a few miles beyond Red Lake where they simply rely on trapping and fishing.
As I said, my file must be a foot thick and it goes back some five or six years. It involves discussions with the board of education of the province because Red Lake is not on reserve territory. It was always my understanding that the Indian affairs branch would welcome a pilot program such as has been urged by the citizens of Red Lake particularly represented by the chamber of commerce under which the buck would not be passed continually between the province and the federal government, the province taking the attitude that these people are basically a federal responsibility and the federal government saying that for a good part of the year the people live off the reserve and thus should be the responsibility of local school board or the province of Ontario.
I have always been assured that the department was willing to make a contribution to what I have called over the years a bridge program under which there would be encouragement for these people to move a few miles south and get employment where industrial developments that have gone north are located. They are the people who should be attracted to employment of this kind but the buck continues to be passed.
We have public schools and separate schools but a very few Indians have been taken into the two schools. I have read speeches of the recent minister of education of the province of Ontario wherein he has said that he feels the Indians of northern Ontario are the responsibility of the province and this responsibility could be taken over by the provincial government. However, we are not getting very far.
I wish now to mention a development of which we should be thoroughly ashamed. Because these children have been neglected a United States church organization, a missionary group-they regard this as a foreign mission-has come in to the civilized northern part of our province and established a school. We should be ashamed of ourselves at having a United States missionary group come in to look after our Indian children. The Amish church missionary group have been running a marvellous school there for four or five years. There is no question of the need for this. Everyone else was washing their hands of the responsibility for these children. The group has carried on the school without assistance from the province, the town or the federal government. I believe the normal capacity of the school is about 40 or 50 children.

In addition to that if the children become neglected as they sometimes do-the parents push oft to their former pursuits in trapping and fishing and leave Red Lake perhaps when employment is not steady for them-they even offer them board and lodging. I believe that compensation has recently been established with respect to the boarding where the parents have gone back to the reserve. I feel that this institution deserves some consideration.
I do not think adequate pressure has been put upon the school authorities of the province, first, to make sure that the truancy laws in so far as Indians are concerned are enforced. They have been ignored, in my opinion, and in consequence if the parents do not deliver their children to school they simply sit there on the outskirts of the Red Lake community with nobody taking responsibility for them and they receive no education. I must give credit to the department in that where it was felt that we could look with confidence to the parents residing fairly steadily at Red Lake a number of the children have been placed in residential schools to the south. This is very much appreciated by me particularly and has relieved the school situation in Red Lake, but it is a very bad situation when everybody says it is somebody else's job.

The hon. member is quite right. It has been a source of considerable concern to the department. The remote areas, of course, bring their own problems and while we could not exactly call Red Lake remote in the sense that some of them are, nevertheless it is not close to any large municipality. However, I am glad the hon. member mentioned it. We have put as many Indians as we could in residential schools. We have done our best also to try to impress upon the municipality and the province what their responsibility is and I do hope we can resolve this difficulty before too long.

Three or four years ago it was indicated to me that as a token of our interest, even though technically those people were not residing on Indian reserves-this was a unique situation-on a voluntary basis for a period of years-I had a term of about five years in mind-with the idea of encouraging the getting to grips with this situation, the department would make a nominal contribution, perhaps what would be the equivalent of the local school board contribution in an unorganized territory, which is about 5 per cent of the over-all cost. Is the department still willing to assist in this matter by making a contribution of that kind?

It is true, that we agreed to that contribution but unfortunately the necessary co-operation was not forthcoming from other quarters.
The minister seems to have a hard time with the government of Ontario.

I should like to ask the minister a question or two, but first of all I hope she can give me some answers to questions asked earlier. I should like to ask her two specific things. One thing which disturbed me, and I suppose the minister, was an accident which occurred last year north of the Winnipeg river when a helicopter crashed. A number of people lost their lives. I know enough about the background of the matter to realize that it was an accident, but there was the question of the necessity of flight at night. We have a long tradition up north that a flight becomes a mercy flight only when it is decided how important the emergency is. I should like to know something of the instructions the doctors have in certain areas as to how important an emergency is?

This is not under my department. Doctors operate under the Department of National Health and Welfare. I do not know whether the hon. member was in the house today when I made my initial statement, but I dealt at some length with the forestry situation. I think the answers to his questions are incorporated in that statement.

I am sorry, I was not in the committee at the time. The minister says that the question of the accident does not come under her department. The point is, as I understand it, two Indians lost their lives in this particular accident. The need, or the urgency, must be spelled out to a certain degree by members of her department or by the Indians themselves. I should like to know where the responsibility lies. We do not want the occurrence of another accident like this one if, as I understand it, to a considerable extent the accident was caused by flying the helicopter at night. There should be some liaison between the two departments that would control these things because mercy flights are all very well but if you are going to risk life to that extent it becomes quite a gamble.
I would agree with the hon. member but I am sorry, Mr. Chairman, the accident to which he refers is not one with which I am familiar. I would have to have more information on it.

The next question I wish to ask the minister has to do with something
5056	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration that has been brought to my attention by people who are attached to forestry companies. The minister knows that whole blocks of land all across the area of northwest Ontario contain trap lines. The minister also knows that the provincial government and the department of lands and forests, I believe, have a number of trapping areas in which Indians get preference. I understand from foresters and other personnel of the bush to whom I have talked that Indians are falling away from these particular jobs, or are tending to let trap lines go. I know that in one particular belt 40 or 45 miles wide, where there are a number of trap lines laid out, I heard last year no one is trapping there at all. I was just wondering whether there is an accelerating pattern right across the north of Indians getting out of trapping and failing to keep going those licensed trap lines set out for them by the provincial government? What is the trend?

The majority of them are operating their trap lines. I think this must be an isolated incident. Again, if I had the particulars of the specific locality and the particular line referred to I might be able to get some information for my hon. friend. But in general the Indians are most anxious to maintain the trap lines so long as they get return from them. I cannot give an answer to the specific line because I do not know.

I will be specific. In the minister's annual report I find the following:
Trapping is still a very important factor in the Indian economy and will be for many years yet. This type of work, arduous though it may be, is accepted by those Indians who have not been in close touch with industrial development.
The point is, I could point out to the minister that my constituency contains almost one third of all Ontario. This might explain to the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi my interest in the Indian vote. You have that large territory, and it is a considerable element in the matter, all the way from Hearst on the east to Sioux Lookout on the west, which is a stretch of over 365 to 370 miles in breadth. I understand that on the north line of the C.N.R. almost all the bush has been taken up and held by the large organizations such as Marathon, Kimberley-Clark, St. Lawrence Corporation, Abitibi, and so on. These firms are operating in this area. I know they are tending to pull Indians away from the trap line. I wanted to know what the trend was, whether anything can be done to keep the Indians in this kind of work or whether we are moving to the stage where in our part of the country we can rule out Indians as trappers?
Mr. Chairman, I would have to check the particular case. I do know that a great many Indians up in that area are working for those companies.
Yes.

Whether they have time to maintain trap lines also is problematical, but I would be very glad to get a report from the superintendent and give the hon. member a detailed report of what is the situation. I can assure him that in the country as a whole the Indians are not losing their interest in trap lines where they still get results from their operation.

Before this is carried I should like the minister to bring us up to date very briefly on this economic development.

We have recently installed as head of the department Mr. Battle whom the hon. member will remember as one of our very valuable staff members, and we now have eight officers working across the country with two more just about to commence operations. Like the hon. member, I am keenly interested in this matter. I think it is a most important part of our administrative work and one that I think is catching on. It is certainly the case that the more employers who use Indian labour the more enthusiasts we have. There is an age-old prejudice involved. We do not know where it got started but it has existed for a long time. However, as employers use Indian labour they find it is a very valuable and worth while move. With the way the division is growing I think we will be able to report very tangible results in a short time.
