The minister says that she has eight officers. Are any of them working in northern and northwestern Ontario?
We do have an officer working in that area.

The minister may be aware that in Longlac there is a fair every fall and a certain amount of support for the fair is received from the Department of Agriculture. I understand they are not

getting any support from the minister's department, but since there is an Indian reserve in juxtaposition to the community and a large number of Indians take an interest in the fair I wonder whether it would be possible for the branch to make a grant to support the fair and perhaps give the Indians an opportunity to play a bigger role in the community.
We will be glad to look into the matter. Our man works out of North Bay. I am told that in our vote we have $200 specifically earmarked for that particular fair.

I think this division is not only attempting to place Indians in positions in industry but also assisting Indians who are still interested in trapping and hunting. For instance, I talked to Mr. Jones last year about getting the Indians in the Fort McPherson and Good Hope areas of the Northwest Territories back into country that has not been utilized for trapping and hunting for many years. He said at that time that money had been set aside and would be spent last year. I am wondering whether the money was spent last year on these projects and whether there is money in the estimates this year to carry on these projects.
There was money spent last year and we have money this year. I can give the hon. member the figures in a moment if he is interested. We have to look them up.

The minister made a reference to North Bay. I think all the officials know it is an old story with me that I continue to be very disappointed at the failure to recognize that North Bay is many hundreds of miles from the part of the country I represent. I think it is 800 or 900 miles away, and in my view it is just nonsense to think that we can operate any more efficiently on a decentralized basis with authority in North Bay than we could if Kenora, the district north of Kenora and the Rainy river district communicated directly with headquarters. It is not the fault of the people at North Bay. It is the matter of the distance and that fact has not been appreciated by somebody in setting up the organizational chart.
In my view North Bay simply constitutes another place where maill is held up because it eventually has to go to headquarters anyway. There are simply not enough days in the few summer months when construction is carried on for the people at North Bay to take the time to travel 800 or 900 miles to Kenora. Many items have to wait to receive the stamp of approval at North Bay before they are sent to headquarters for a further

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration stamp of approval. In my opinion the North Bay office is just another post office that holds up things. I feel that geography is being ignored and that if we have to have a decentralized organization there certainly should be a regional office much nearer to the field. I referred to the distance of 800 or 900 miles. We have no high school accommodation and our Indian children have to be sent 800 or 900 miles for a high school education. Separation from families on a basis of that kind is completely unsound.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to hold up my own estimates but I should like to tell the committee about a very interesting experiment that we are initiating this year. I have long felt that there is tremendous artistic talent of many kinds among our Indian children. As hon. members know, we have had a scholarship fund but heretofore scholarships have been awarded from the fund in the scholastic field and for vocational training, nursing and so on.
I became very much interested in the possibilities for artists, musicians and others who might have special talent which would not be covered particularly by the usual definition of scholarship. I am happy to say that among the 17 scholarships awarded in the past year there were two granted to artists and two to musicians. I was very pleased about this and I got in touch with some friends of mine who are in the music business. The outcome of our negotiations is that we have made arrangements with the Royal Conservatory of Music, and with their very generous co-operation their examiners, when they are in the field from coast to coast, will adjudicate for us with respect to individual students who are recommended to us at the local level as having particular talent.
By this means we hope to encourage and bring forward young people with exceptional talent at a time when encouragement and training will do them some good. We are also exploring the art field in the same manner. I thought the committee might like to know that a special effort is being made to try to help these young people who have specific talents in the arts and educate them at a time of life when they need this help.

What progress is being made toward the integration of Indians in the ordinary public schools of Canada? I know this move has been under way for a number
5058	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration of years. Would the minister also explain what is meant in the details on pages 148 and 149 by employees listed as teacher aides? There are 37 of them in the day schools and 52 in the residential schools and also 13 part-time teacher aides in the residential schools. Exactly what do these people do?

I wonder if the minister would care to comment on the wage levels and the supply? I notice the wage levels are well below the wage levels of the ordinary public school teachers, at least in Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia, and I imagine also Ontario.

No, teachers.

Is the minister claiming that the wages paid to teachers in Indian schools vary from province to province?
No, ours is an over-all standard, but it is based on the average of the salaries paid across the country by the various provinces.

May I then ask, how is the department making out with the recruitment of teachers in Ontario, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia? Does this particular matter have any relationship to the engagement of so-called teacher aides?

No, there is no relationship there, Mr. Chairman. The work of teacher aides, while it is useful to us, is largely one of training. When you get into the provinces the hon. member has enumerated the salaries are probably higher than in some of the other provinces and it is true we do have difficulty in recruiting teachers. However, I do not believe the difficulty has been so severe that we have been unable to staff our classrooms.
In some of the provinces of Canada our teachers are probably making more than the


average teacher in the province. As the hon. member knows, we are governed by federal rules and we cannot have different wage scales in different provinces.
I wonder if the minister would answer the other query as to what headway is being made in the question of integration of Indians into the regular public school system?

Again, I believe I gave that information in my initial statement. Last year, 1958-59, the number of Indian children attending non-Indian schools was 8,186, and this year, 1959-60, it was 9,479 or 1,300 more.

No, Mr. Chairman.

We are not making much progress. It is over three years since the department itself said the boilers in the residential school at Fort Frances were in such condition that repairs were not economically justified. No start has as yet been made on that building. During the last two winters we have had heavy unemployment and the work would have been useful to the community. I would hope that in the near future the minister could give some indication that the project is going ahead.
The other problem is the accommodation at Sioux Lookout which, I am told, is not adequate for the children of that area. I understand they are turning down now as many pupils as they have registered. They do not particularly want the continuation of that school. They very fairly state that perhaps the proper place for another school would be midway between that school and Kenora. will be glad to do our best to give them a little prod. In so far as the circumstances at Sioux Lookout are concerned, I must say that I am not aware of this but I will have a look at it.

I just want to make one final observation. I notice that the wages of teachers in residential schools are listed at $2,700 as a minimum. At the same time, I notice that a handyman in the residential school receives $3,100; kitchen helpers receive a reasonable wage; a labourer is listed at $2,800; a laundress at $2,800 and a seamstress also at $2,800. Perhaps the minister could look at that. I would hope the minister would agree that these teachers' wages are in need of a revision upward and at a very early date because I can well imagine the quality of teachers the minister is able to obtain in the four provinces I mentioned. I regret that Indian education is going to bear the brunt of it. I feel that a teacher's beginning wage certainly ought to exceed the wages of a seamstress, laundress, labourer or handyman.
